q1.question: Are there any hidden fees with Lumi?
q1.answer: No. You pay a transparent 2% fee on each transaction — that's it. No subscription fees, no withdrawal charges, no currency conversion markups. The rate you see is the rate you get.

q2.question: How does Lumi's rate compare to my bank?
q2.answer: European banks typically charge 1.5–3% in foreign transaction fees plus a currency markup of 2–5%. With airport exchanges, the spread can reach 8–10%. Lumi uses near-interbank rates with a single 2% fee, saving you up to €120 per €1,000 spent compared to the worst alternatives.

q3.question: Is there a minimum or maximum amount I can pay?
q3.answer: You can make payments from as little as €1. There are no minimum transaction requirements. Maximum limits depend on your account verification level and local regulations.

A1.a: Lumi is for EU and EEA residents travelling in Southeast Asia: holidaymakers, backpackers, business travellers and digital nomads. You only need a euro bank account (SEPA) in your own name.
A1.aka: Is Lumi for tourists? / Can expats or digital nomads use it?

A2.a: Lumi is a brand of Lumifin SAS, a French technology company. Payments and fund movements are carried out by regulated, licensed payment partners in Europe and Asia.
A2.aka: Which company owns Lumi? / Is Lumi French?

A3.a: No crypto knowledge is needed. Lumi uses stablecoins to move funds from your home country to Vietnam. You top up your wallet in euros, and your funds are converted and settled in the local currency, which you can then use to pay merchants via QR codes.
A3.aka: Do I hold crypto? / Is this stablecoins? / Do I need a crypto wallet?

A4.q: Why use Lumi instead of cash or my card?
A4.a: Lumi lets you pay using QR codes at participating merchants across Vietnam, including shops, street stalls and taxis. Unlike cash or foreign bank cards, Lumi offers a convenient way to pay in local currency. A 2% fee applies, and the exchange rate is shown before you pay.
A4.aka: Why not just use my bank card? / Is it cheaper than an ATM?

A5.a: Yes. The app is free and there's no monthly plan. You only pay the fee shown on each payment.
A5.aka: How much does the app cost? / Is there a subscription?

A6.a: Lumi is live in Vietnam. We are still adding features, so you may see occasional changes. Tell us about any problem in the in-app chat and it goes straight to the team.
A6.aka: Is the app finished? / Is Lumi still in beta? / Why does it say beta?

A7.q: Which phones does Lumi work on?
A7.a: Lumi is available on iOS and Android. You need a phone with a working camera to scan QR codes.
A7.aka: Is there an iPhone app? / Android? / Can I use it on a tablet?

E1.q: Can I use Lumi if I live in the UK or Switzerland?
E1.a: Not yet. The UK and Switzerland aren't supported for now. Leave your email at lumifin.io and we'll tell you when they are.
E1.aka: UK resident? / Swiss bank account? / GBP or CHF?

E2.q: Can I use Lumi if I'm from the US, Canada, India or Australia?
E2.a: Not yet. Lumi currently serves EU and EEA residents only.
E2.aka: I'm not European, can I join?

E3.q: I'm an EU citizen living outside Europe. Can I sign up?
E3.a: All you need to use Lumi is a European bank account in your own name. Your nationality or country of residence does not determine your eligibility.
E3.aka: I'm French but live in Vietnam / Do I need to live in Europe?

E4.q: Can I use a Revolut, N26 or Wise euro account?
E4.a: Yes, as long as it's a euro account with an IBAN in the SEPA zone and in your own name.
E4.aka: Do neobanks work? / Can I top up from Wise EUR?

E5.q: Can I use someone else's bank account?
E5.a: No. Money must come from a personal account in your own name, and the name must match your verified identity. Transfers from other people's or business accounts may be rejected and returned.
E5.aka: Can my partner top up for me? / Joint account? / Company account?

E6.q: How old do I need to be?
E6.aka: Can my teenager use Lumi? / Minimum age?

E7.a: Most people finish in about 3-5 minutes. Identity checks are usually quick, but some need a manual review.
E7.aka: How fast can I start paying?

E8.q: Should I set up Lumi before I travel?
E8.a: The best way to prepare for your trip is to create your Lumi account and complete your first top-up before you travel. You can also purchase an eSIM directly through Lumi so you have mobile data as soon as you land in Vietnam. You can sign up while abroad too, as long as you have an internet connection.
E8.aka: Can I sign up once I'm in Vietnam?

E9.q: Can I have more than one Lumi account?
E9.a: No. Each person can have one account. If you've lost access to yours, contact support rather than opening a new one.
E9.aka: Second account / New account with another email

E10.q: I didn't receive my sign-up email or code. What should I do?
E10.a: Check your spam folder and that the email or number is correct, then tap resend after a minute. If it still doesn't arrive, contact support@lumifin.io with the email you used.
E10.aka: No OTP / Verification code not arriving / No SMS

V1.q: The app selected the wrong country for my document. What do I do?
V1.a: Change the country manually on the document step before taking photos. If you can't change it, close the app, reopen it and start again. Contact support if it keeps happening.
V1.aka: It shows India instead of France / Wrong country in verification

V2.q: Can I use Lumi before I'm verified?
V2.a: You can create your account and explore the app, but adding money, paying and using rewards need verification first.
V2.aka: Can I add money without verifying?

V3.a: Your documents are processed by a specialist identity-verification provider, encrypted, and stored in the EU. We only use them to verify you and meet legal obligations. See our privacy policy for details.
V3.aka: What do you do with my passport photo? / Who sees my selfie?

V4.q: Do I need to verify again later?
V4.a: Sometimes, for example if your ID expires, your details change or a regulatory check requires it. We'll tell you in the app if we need anything.
V4.aka: Re-verification / Why are you asking for ID again?

S1.a: On the login screen tap "Forgot password", enter your account email, and follow the link we send. Check spam if it doesn't arrive within a few minutes.

S2.q: Why do I keep getting logged out?
S2.a: For security, Lumi signs you out after a period of inactivity or when it sees a new device. Make sure you're on the latest app version. If it happens every time you open the app, tell us in the in-app chat.
S2.aka: App asks me to log in again / Re-authenticate every time

S3.q: Why am I asked to verify this device?
S3.a: When you log in on a new phone, or after resetting security details, we send a one-time code to confirm it's really you.
S3.aka: Code to verify device / New phone

S4.q: I changed my phone. How do I move my account?
S4.a: Install Lumi on the new phone, log in with your email and password, and confirm the one-time code. Your balance and history move with your account. Then set your mPIN again.
S4.aka: New phone / Transfer Lumi to new device

S5.q: My phone was lost or stolen. What should I do?
S5.a: Contact support@lumifin.io or WhatsApp +33 6 19 78 42 22 right away so we can secure your account. Change your email password too. Your funds can't be spent without your mPIN or biometrics.

S6.q: I see a payment I didn't make.
S6.a: Contact support immediately with the date and amount. We'll secure your account and investigate. Don't share codes or your mPIN with anyone who contacts you.
S6.aka: Unauthorised transaction / Fraud / Someone used my account

S7.q: Will Lumi ever ask for my mPIN or codes?
S7.a: Never. Lumi staff will never ask for your mPIN, password or one-time codes. If someone does, it's a scam. Report it to support@lumifin.io.
S7.aka: Is this message from Lumi? / Phishing

S8.q: Can I use Lumi with a VPN?
S8.a: Lumi works without a VPN in supported countries. If you're having trouble connecting, try switching between Wi-Fi and mobile data.
S8.aka: VPN blocks login / App not working abroad

T1.q: Can I top up with a debit or credit card?
T1.a: Not yet. You can top up by SEPA transfer or open banking from a European bank account. Card top-ups are coming soon.

T2.q: Can I use Apple Pay or Google Pay?
T2.a: Not at the moment. You can add money to your Lumi wallet using a SEPA transfer or by selecting “Connect to my bank” in the app.

T3.q: Can I top up with crypto or stablecoins?
T3.a: No. Lumi only accepts euros from a bank account in your name.

T4.q: I forgot to add the payment reference.
T4.a: You don't need to add a payment reference when making a SEPA transfer to Lumi. If your transfer hasn't appeared in your Lumi wallet, contact us through the in-app chat or WhatsApp with the transfer amount, date, sending IBAN and a screenshot of the transfer so we can investigate.
T4.aka: Wrong reference / No reference on transfer

T5.a: You need to register the IBAN displayed in the Lumi app as a new beneficiary in your mobile banking app. Some banks may require you to wait up to 1 working day before you can make the transfer. If the transfer is still declined, please contact your bank for assistance.
T5.aka: Open banking failed / Bank blocked the transfer

T6.q: Can I top up from a bank account in someone else's name?
T6.a: No. Top-ups must come from a personal account in your own name. Transfers from other accounts may be returned.

T7.q: How much should I load for my trip?
T7.a: We recommend checking travel guides or forums to estimate your budget for Vietnam based on your trip length and spending plans. You can start by topping up 50–75% of your estimated expenses and add more to your Lumi wallet whenever you need.
T7.aka: How much money do I need in Vietnam?

T8.q: Can I add money while I'm abroad?
T8.a: Yes. You can top up from anywhere with an internet connection, as long as the money comes from your euro account.
T8.aka: Top up from Vietnam / Top up on holiday

P1.q: Which QR codes can I scan?
P1.a: In Vietnam, Lumi supports QR payments for foreign visitors through eligible VietQR codes and QR codes from supported Vietnamese banks or wallets. Not all QR codes are compatible, as Lumi is designed for foreign users paying local merchants.
P1.aka: What does a supported QR look like? / Which logo should I look for?

P2.q: Why does the amount sometimes fill in automatically?
P2.a: Some QR codes include the amount (common at checkouts and on bills), so Lumi fills it in. Printed QR codes on stands usually don't, so you type the amount yourself. Always check it before confirming.
P2.aka: Static vs dynamic QR / Do I type the amount?

P3.q: Can I pay a street vendor or market stall?
P3.a: Yes, you can pay at street vendors, market stalls and small shops in Vietnam, provided they display a supported QR code. Personal and individual bank QR codes are also supported in Vietnam.
P3.aka: Small shops / Personal QR / Night market

P4.q: The cashier wants to scan my phone. Can I pay that way?
P4.a: Not yet. Lumi works by you scanning the merchant's QR code. If the shop only scans customers' codes, ask if they have a QR you can scan, or use another payment method.
P4.aka: Show my QR / Cashier scans me / 7-Eleven

P5.q: Can I pay online or in apps like Grab?
P5.a: Lumi is built for paying merchant QR codes in person. If a website or app shows a supported QR at checkout, you can scan it from another screen.
P5.aka: Pay on a website / Grab / Shopee / Booking

P6.q: Can I pay bills or utility QR codes?
P6.a: Hotel and restaurant payments can be made using supported merchant QR codes. Utility bills and other biller QR codes may not be supported. Please contact us if you're unsure whether a QR code is compatible with Lumi.

P7.q: Can I pay a taxi or motorbike driver?
P7.a: Yes, if the driver shows a supported QR code. Many drivers in Vietnam have a bank QR on a card or their phone.
P7.aka: Xe om / Taxi / Grab driver QR

P8.q: How do I show the merchant that I've paid?
P8.a: After payment you'll see a confirmation screen with the amount, merchant and time. Show it to the merchant; their app also shows the payment arrive. Every receipt stays in your transaction history.

P9.q: Can I split a bill or pay a friend?
P9.a: Lumi doesn't have friend-to-friend transfers. If your friend has a local bank business or personal QR in a supported country, you can scan and pay it like a merchant.
P9.aka: Send money to a friend / Pay someone back / P2P

P10.q: Can I receive money into Lumi?
P10.a: No. Lumi is for paying, not receiving. Your balance can only be topped up from your own euro bank account.
P10.aka: Can friends send me money? / Receive payment

P11.a: Yes. Just include the tip in the amount you enter when you scan the QR code.

P12.q: Can I cancel a payment after confirming it?
P12.a: No. QR payments go straight to the merchant's account and can't be cancelled once confirmed. Always check the amount and merchant name before you confirm.

W1.a: Not yet. Thailand is coming soon. Sign up for updates and we'll tell you when it's live.

W2.q: Does Lumi work in Indonesia or Bali?
W2.a: Not yet. Indonesia is coming soon. Sign up for updates and we'll tell you when it's live.

W3.a: After Thailand and Indonesia, the roadmap includes Malaysia, Cambodia, the Philippines, Laos, South Korea, Taiwan and Mongolia. We'll announce each one when it goes live.

W4.q: How do I know if a shop accepts Lumi?
W4.a: If the shop displays a VietQR code, or a QR from a Vietnamese bank at the till, you can usually pay with Lumi. Shops don't need to sign up to anything.
W4.aka: Will this shop take Lumi? / Which merchants?

W5.q: Can I use Lumi in Europe or at home?
W5.a: No. Lumi is for paying QR codes in supported Southeast Asian countries.
W5.aka: Pay in France / Use Lumi in my country

W6.q: I'm going to a country Lumi doesn't support yet. Can I still use it?
W6.a: Your balance stays safe in your account, but you can't pay QR codes there yet. Use a card or cash in those countries and pay with Lumi again once you're back in Vietnam.
W6.aka: Not supported country / Travelling to Thailand next week

W7.q: Can I request a new country?
W7.a: Yes. Tell us in the in-app chat or at support@lumifin.io. Requests help us decide where to launch next.

R1.q: Why is the rate different from the one on Google?
R1.a: Google shows the mid-market rate, which moves every few seconds and isn't available to consumers. Lumi's rate is live, close to it, and fixed once you see the confirmation screen.

R2.q: Is Lumi cheaper than my bank card?
R2.a: Usually, yes. European banks often charge 1.5–3% per foreign card payment plus a 2–5% exchange margin, and ATMs add withdrawal fees. On €1,000 of spending, Lumi costs about €20 in fees, versus €60–144 with cards, ATMs or airport exchange.
R2.aka: Compare with card / Is it worth it?

R3.q: Will my bank charge me for using Lumi abroad?
R3.a: SEPA transfers in euros within Europe are generally free of transfer fees. However, fees may depend on your bank and account type, so check with your bank if you're unsure.

R4.q: Does the merchant pay a fee?
R4.a: The merchant receives the full amount in local currency, just as if a local had paid.
R4.aka: Does the shop lose money? / Merchant charge

R5.q: Does the exchange rate change between scanning and paying?
R5.a: The rate is shown on the confirmation screen and applies when you confirm. If you leave the screen open for a long time, it may refresh to the latest rate.

R6.q: Should I pay in euros or local currency if a shop offers both?
R6.a: With Lumi you always pay in local currency and the conversion is done by Lumi, so this choice doesn't come up. On card terminals, always choose local currency; paying in euros there usually costs more.
R6.aka: Pay in EUR on card terminal / Dynamic currency conversion

L1.q: What's the smallest payment I can make?
L1.a: The minimum payment in Vietnam is 10,000 VND (approximately €0.33), so you can use Lumi for small purchases like a coffee or a street-food snack.
L1.aka: Minimum payment / Can I pay for a coffee?

L2.q: Is there a maximum per payment?
L2.a: Yes. max per payment in 3,000,000 VND
L2.aka: Per-transaction limit / Can I pay my hotel?

L3.q: Is there a daily or monthly limit?
L3.a: Yes. daily limit is 6,000,000 VND and monthly limit is 25,000,000 VND for payments and for top-ups daily limit is 600 EUR and monthly 3000 EUR

L5.q: My payment was declined for exceeding a limit. What can I do?
L5.a: Split the amount into two payments if the merchant agrees, or wait until your daily limit resets.

L6.a: No. We are working on it.

F1.q: My payment failed. What should I do?
F1.a:
Please check that:

- You have enough money in your Lumi wallet to cover the payment, including the 2% fee.
- You're connected to the internet.
- You're using the latest version of the Lumi app.

Then try scanning the QR code again. If the payment still fails, contact us through the in-app chat or on WhatsApp for assistance.
F1.aka: Payment didn't go through / Transaction failed / Error when paying

F2.q: My payment says pending. What does that mean?
F2.a: Sometimes the local bank network takes longer to confirm. The amount is held while we check. If the payment went through, it changes to completed; if it didn't, the full amount returns to your balance. If you face any problem, contact support.

F3.q: The money left my balance but the merchant says they didn't receive it.
F3.a: Don't pay again yet. Show the merchant your receipt; their bank app can take a moment to update. If they still don't see it, contact support with the receipt, merchant name and time, and we'll trace it. If the payment didn't reach them, you'll get your money back.
F3.aka: Merchant didn't get paid / Shop says not received

F4.q: My payment failed but money was taken from my balance.
F4.a: If a payment fails after money is held, it's returned to your balance automatically. If you don't see it back within that time, contact support.
F4.aka: Charged but failed / Deducted but declined

F5.a: Contact support with both receipts or a screenshot of your history. We'll check with the payment network and refund any duplicate.

F6.q: Can I get a refund for something I bought?
F6.a: Refunds for goods or services are between you and the merchant, as with cash. Lumi can't send money back to your wallet from a merchant. Ask them for a cash refund.
F6.aka: Return an item / Merchant refund / Cancel order

F7.a: Clean your camera lens, turn up screen brightness if scanning from a phone, and hold steady about 15 cm away. Make sure it's a payment QR, not a menu, Wi-Fi or app-download code. Still stuck? Ask the merchant for another QR.
F7.aka: Scanner not working / Camera won't read QR

F8.q: Lumi says the QR code isn't supported.
F8.a: The code may be from a country or network Lumi doesn't support yet, a non-payment QR, or a format we don't accept (such as some utility or personal-wallet codes). Ask the merchant if they have a VietQR or bank QR.
F8.aka: Unsupported QR / Invalid QR / This QR can't be paid

F9.a: Some payments are stopped by automatic security checks to protect you. Check your balance and retry once. If it's blocked again, contact support. For security we can't share the details of these checks.
F9.aka: Payment blocked for security / Transaction declined for security

F10.q: Payments fail late at night. Why?
F10.a: Some local banks run maintenance late at night, which can briefly stop payments. Try again after a few minutes, or pay another way. No money is taken for a failed payment.
F10.aka: Payment fails after midnight / Bank maintenance

F11.q: I'm using an old version of the app and something's missing.
F11.a: Please update Lumi to the latest version available on your app store to access the latest features and improvements. If you're still experiencing issues, contact us through the in-app chat or on WhatsApp for assistance.
F11.aka: My app has no rewards / Feature missing / Old build

F12.q: What should I send support about a payment problem?
F12.a: Your account email, the date and time, the amount, the merchant name, and a screenshot of the receipt or error. This lets us trace it in one go.

WD1.q: What happens to my balance after my trip?
WD1.a: Your balance stays in your Lumi account, ready for your next trip; it doesn't expire. You can also withdraw it to your bank account whenever you like.
WD1.aka: Leftover money / Money left after holiday

WD2.q: Can I withdraw to a different bank account?
WD2.a: You can withdraw funds only to a European bank account held in your own name.

WD3.q: Can I withdraw cash at an ATM with Lumi?
WD3.a: No. Lumi has no card, so it can't be used at ATMs. It's designed so you need much less cash.

WD4.q: Can I move my Lumi balance to another person?
WD4.a: No. Your balance can only be spent by you or returned to your own bank account.
WD4.aka: Give my balance to a friend / Transfer to someone else

RW2.q: I didn't receive my coupon or reward.
RW2.a: Please check that you've met the eligibility requirements for the offer and that you're using the latest version of the Lumi app. If your coupon or reward is still missing, contact us through the in-app chat or WhatsApp for assistance.
RW2.aka: Welcome bonus missing / Where's my reward?

RW3.q: Where do I find my rewards?
RW3.a: Open the Rewards section in the app. You'll see your active coupons, rewards earned and a field to enter a code.

RW4.q: How do I use a promo code or coupon?
RW4.a: In the Rewards section, tap Enter code, type it exactly as given and tap Apply. Codes only work once your identity is verified. Each code has its own conditions and expiry date.
RW4.aka: Enter coupon / Redeem code / Promo code not working

RW5.a: Check the spelling and expiry date, and that your identity verification is complete. Some codes are one per person or only for new users. If you think it should work, send the code to support.
RW5.aka: Invalid code / Code expired / Code already used

RW6.q: How does the referral programme work?
RW6.a: Share your referral code from the app. When your friend signs up with it and meets the conditions, you both get a reward.
RW6.aka: Invite friends / Refer a friend / Referral code

RW7.q: My friend signed up but I didn't get my referral reward.
RW7.a: Rewards are paid once your friend completes all the steps, such as verification and a first top-up or payment. If they have and it's still missing, contact support with their sign-up email.

RW10.a: Each reward shows its expiry date in the Rewards section. Use it before then; expired rewards can't be restored.

RW11.q: Can I withdraw my reward credit?
RW11.a: No. Reward credit can only be spent on Lumi payments.
RW11.aka: Cash out bonus / Transfer welcome credit

RW12.q: I'm a venue owner or influencer. Can I partner with Lumi?
RW12.a: Yes. Lumifriends is our programme for venues and creators in Vietnam. Contact us at info@lumifin.io to learn more.

X1.a: eSIMs are coming soon. You'll be able to buy a local data plan in the app and activate it before you land, with no physical SIM.
X1.aka: Data plan / Mobile internet in Vietnam / SIM card

X2.q: Will my phone work with a Lumi eSIM?
X2.a: Your phone must support eSIM and be unlocked. Most recent iPhones, Pixels and Samsung Galaxy models do. Check your phone settings or ask your carrier.
X2.aka: eSIM compatible? / Is my phone unlocked?

X3.q: When should I install the eSIM?
X3.a: install before departure, activation on arrival.
X3.aka: Install before travel? / Activate on arrival

X4.q: Can I get a refund on an eSIM?
X4.a: If we fail to provide an esim to you, you will recieve the refund

X5.q: How do I pay for an eSIM?
X5.a: You can directly pay from Lumi wallet

X6.q: What are daily tours and restaurant offers?
X6.a: We're adding curated tours and local restaurant offers you can book or unlock with Lumi soon.

M1.a: Yes, you can download the full statement from the transactions page.
M1.aka: Export transactions / PDF statement / Expense report

M2.q: How do I turn notifications on or off?
M2.a: Manage push notifications in your phone's settings for Lumi. Security alerts, such as new logins or mPIN locks, are always sent. You can unsubscribe from marketing emails using the link in any email.

M3.q: Why has my account been suspended or restricted?
M3.a: Accounts can be restricted after a security alert, a failed check, or a request for more information. Contact support@lumifin.io and we'll explain what's needed. For legal reasons we can't always share every detail.
M3.aka: Account frozen / Account blocked / Can't use my account

M4.q: How do I close or delete my account?
M4.aka: Delete account / Cancel Lumi / Remove my data

M5.q: What happens to my data after I close my account?
M5.a: We delete what we can. Identity and transaction records must be kept for a set period under anti-money-laundering law.
M5.aka: Data retention / Do you keep my data?

M6.q: Can I reopen a closed account?
M6.a: Contact support and we'll help. You may need to verify your identity again.

G1.a: Lumi is a brand of Lumifin SAS, a technology company. Lumifin is registered as a Money Services Business (MSB) in Canada. Payment services are provided by licensed payment partners.

G2.q: Is my money protected by deposit insurance?
G2.a: Your funds are safeguarded by a regulated payment partner that holds an electronic money licence in Europe.
G2.aka: Deposit guarantee / FGDR / Is it insured?

G4.q: Do I need to keep a recovery phrase or private key?
G4.a: No. You log in with your email, password and mPIN. There's no recovery phrase to store and no crypto keys to manage.

G5.q: How does Lumi use my personal data?
G5.a: We use your data only to run your account, verify your identity, process payments and meet legal duties. We don't sell your data. You can read the full privacy policy at lumifin.io/en/privacy.
G5.aka: Privacy / GDPR / Do you sell my data?

G6.q: How do I get a copy of my data or ask for it to be deleted?
G6.a: Email support@lumifin.io with your request. Under GDPR you can access, correct or delete your data, subject to records we must keep by law.

G8.q: What isn't Lumi allowed to be used for?
G8.a: You can't use Lumi for anything illegal, for gambling, to move money for other people, or from or to sanctioned countries. Accounts used this way are closed. See the terms at lumifin.io/en/terms.

G9.q: How do I spot a fake Lumi message or website?
G9.a: Our only website is lumifin.io and we'll never ask for your mPIN, password or one-time codes. Only download Lumi from the official app stores. Forward anything suspicious to support@lumifin.io.

C1.a: Our support hours are designed to accommodate our users in Europe and Vietnam. You can contact us through the in-app chat or WhatsApp, and we'll get back to you as soon as possible during support hours.
C1.aka: When can I reach you? / Is support 24 / 7?

C2.a:
During support hours, our team aims to respond based on the priority of your request: critical issues within 60 minutes, high-priority issues within 2 hours, normal queries within 8 hours, and low-priority requests within 2 business days.

Resolution times may range from the same day to 3 business days, depending on the issue. Messages received outside support hours will be addressed during the next support period. Thank you for your patience and understanding!
C2.aka: Response time / Still waiting for a reply

C3.q: How do I give feedback or report a bug?
C3.a: We'd love to hear it. Send it in the in-app chat with a screenshot if you can. Your feedback goes straight to the product team.

C4.q: How do I make a complaint?
C4.a: Email support@lumifin.io with "Complaint" in the subject and the details.

C5.q: Bot fallback: I don't understand the question
C5.a: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Try asking in a few words, like "top up", "payment failed" or "fees". Or type "agent" to reach our team.

C6.q: Bot fallback: hand-off to a person
C6.a: I'll connect you with our team. To help them, please share your account email and, for a payment issue, the date, amount and a screenshot.

esim.subtitle: Buy an eSIM in the Lumi app, install it before you fly, and land with working mobile data. No physical SIM to swap, no queue at the airport, no roaming bill when you get home.
esim.howIntro: Four steps, and only the first one needs doing before you fly.

steps.title: Pick a plan in the app
steps.desc: Open Lumi, choose your destination and how much data you want. You pay from your Lumi balance, in euros, with the price shown before you confirm.

steps.title: Install the eSIM
steps.desc: The app walks you through it. Installing takes a couple of minutes and needs Wi-Fi, so do it at home before you fly rather than at the airport.

steps.title: Switch it on when you land
steps.desc: Turn on the Lumi line in your phone settings as you land. Data starts working straight away — no shop, no queue, no paper SIM to lose.

steps.desc: Running low? Add more data from the app in a few taps. Nothing to collect and no need to find a phone shop.

esim.whyH: Why an eSIM beats the alternatives

benefits.title: No physical SIM to swap
benefits.desc: An eSIM is built into your phone. Nothing to collect, nothing to lose, and your home SIM stays exactly where it is.

benefits.title: Keep your own number
benefits.desc: Your normal number stays active for calls and texts while the eSIM handles data. Bank codes and messages still reach you.

benefits.title: No surprise roaming bill
benefits.desc: You pay up front for a set amount of data. When it runs out, it stops — there is no bill waiting for you at home.

benefits.title: Working from the moment you land
benefits.desc: No hunting for a shop, no passport photocopies, no queue at arrivals. Order a Grab before you leave the terminal.

benefits.title: Paid from your Lumi balance
benefits.desc: The same euro balance you use for QR payments, with the rate shown up front. One app rather than another card payment abroad.

benefits.title: Top up in seconds
benefits.desc: If you run out mid-trip you add more from the app. No need to find a counter that sells top-up vouchers.

esim.plansIntro: The eSIM follows the same roadmap as Lumi payments: Vietnam first, with the rest of Southeast Asia close behind.
esim.plansNote: Live prices and data amounts are shown in the app before you pay. Prices vary by destination and plan size.

faqs.a: A SIM card built into your phone rather than a piece of plastic you slot in. You install it by scanning a code or tapping a link, and your phone can hold several at once — so a travel eSIM sits alongside your normal SIM instead of replacing it.

Most phones from roughly 2019 onwards do, including iPhone XS and newer, Google Pixel 3 and newer, and recent Samsung Galaxy S and Z models. Look in Settings for an option to add an eSIM or a second mobile plan. If your phone has no such option, it does not support eSIM and a travel eSIM will not work.

faqs.q: Will I keep my normal phone number?
faqs.a: Yes. The eSIM handles data only, and your usual SIM stays active for calls and texts. That matters if your bank sends verification codes by SMS.

faqs.q: Should I install it before or after I fly?
faqs.a: Before. Installing needs an internet connection, which is exactly what you will not have at arrivals. Install at home on Wi-Fi, then simply switch the line on when you land.

faqs.q: Do I need to be online to use it once installed?
faqs.a: No. Installation needs Wi-Fi, but after that the eSIM connects to the local network by itself as soon as you arrive and switch it on.

faqs.q: Does it include calls and texts?
faqs.a: The plans are data only. You can still call and message over the internet with WhatsApp, Zalo, FaceTime or anything similar, and your home SIM handles normal calls if you leave it switched on.

faqs.q: What happens when my data runs out?
faqs.a: The connection stops rather than rolling into expensive charges. You can top up from the app in a few taps and carry on.

faqs.q: Can I use it as a hotspot for my laptop?
faqs.a: On most phones yes, and it is a common way to work from a café. Check the plan details in the app, as tethering is occasionally restricted by the local network.

faqs.q: Can I use one eSIM across several countries?
faqs.a: Vietnam is the first destination at launch. Regional plans covering several Southeast Asian countries are planned — the app always shows which countries a plan covers before you buy.

faqs.q: Can I get a refund if I do not use it?
faqs.a: Write to us at info@lumifin.io before you install it and we will look at it case by case. Once an eSIM has been installed and activated it generally cannot be refunded, which is standard across eSIM providers.

faqs.q: Do I need a Lumi account to buy one?
faqs.a: Yes. The eSIM is bought from your Lumi balance in the app, so you need an account and a topped-up wallet. Eligibility is the same as for payments: EU and EEA residents with a SEPA bank account.

esim.ctaBody: Download Lumi and we will let you know the moment the eSIM goes live.

section1.title: 1. Data Controller
section1.body1: LumiFin SAS ("Lumi", "we", "us") is the data controller for processing described in this Privacy Policy. Address: 50 rue Anatole France, 92290 Châtenay-Malabry, France. Email: privacy@lumifin.io.

sub1.title: 2.1 Data you provide
sub1.item1: Account registration: full name, email address, phone number, date of birth, nationality, residential address.

sub2.item3: Usage data: screens viewed, features used, session duration (collected via Firebase Analytics).

sub3.title: 2.3 Data from third parties
sub3.body: Identity verification results from our KYC provider; payment confirmation data from Transfi; Open Banking account information from our payment initiation provider (limited to IBAN verification).

section3.title: 3. Purposes and Legal Bases
section3.intro: We process your personal data for the following purposes and legal bases under Article 6 GDPR:
section3.item1: Contract performance (Art. 6(1)(b)): creating and managing your Account; processing transactions; displaying balance and history; communicating about your Account and transactions; providing customer support.
section3.item2: Legal obligations (Art. 6(1)(c)): identity verification and KYC/AML compliance (French Monetary and Financial Code, Art. L561-12); responding to lawful requests from authorities; maintaining records as required by law.
section3.item3: Legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f)): preventing fraud and securing the App; improving our services and user experience; analytics and crash reporting (via Firebase Analytics and Firebase Crashlytics); enforcing our Terms and Conditions.
section3.item4: Consent (Art. 6(1)(a)): marketing communications (you can withdraw consent at any time); optional co-marketing communications from Lumi and Transfi (opt-in only).

section4.title: 4. Data Sharing
section4.intro: We share personal data only when necessary and with appropriate safeguards:
section4.item1: Payment Partner (Transfi): We share your identity, financial, and transaction data with Transfi so they can provide Payment Services. Transfi processes this data as an independent controller under its own privacy policy and legal bases.
section4.item2: Service providers: We use third-party processors for identity verification, analytics (Firebase), crash reporting (Firebase Crashlytics), cloud hosting, Open Banking payment initiation, and customer support tools. These processors act on our instructions under Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) that include GDPR-compliant safeguards.
section4.item3: Legal requirements: We may disclose data to authorities when required by law, regulation, or court order.
section4.outro: We do not sell your personal data. We do not use your data for automated decision-making or profiling that produces legal effects.

section5.title: 5. International Transfers
section5.body: Some of our service providers and Transfi operate outside the EU/EEA. When personal data is transferred internationally, we ensure adequate protection through: EU adequacy decisions (where applicable); Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) approved by the European Commission; the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (for US-based processors certified under the DPF).
section5.outro: You may request a copy of the relevant transfer safeguards by contacting privacy@lumifin.io.

section6.title: 6. Data Retention
section6.intro: We retain your data only as long as necessary for the purposes described:
section6.item1: Account data: retained while your Account is active plus 30 days after closure to handle disputes.
section6.item2: Identity documents (KYC): 5 years from end of relationship, as required by French AML law (Art. L561-12 CMF).
section6.item3: Transaction records: 5 to 10 years depending on applicable legal retention requirements (tax, AML, accounting).
section6.item4: Security logs: up to 24 months for fraud prevention and incident investigation.
section6.item5: Analytics data: 14 months (Firebase Analytics default retention).
section6.item6: Marketing suppression list: retained indefinitely to honour your opt-out.
section6.outro: After the applicable retention period, data is securely deleted or anonymized.

section7.title: 7. Your Rights
section7.intro: Under the GDPR, you have the following rights regarding your personal data:
section7.rights: Right of access (Art. 15): obtain a copy of your data. Right to rectification (Art. 16): correct inaccurate data. Right to erasure (Art. 17): request deletion (subject to legal retention obligations). Right to restriction (Art. 18): limit processing in certain circumstances. Right to data portability (Art. 20): receive your data in a machine-readable format. Right to object (Art. 21): object to processing based on legitimate interests. Right to withdraw consent (Art. 7(3)): withdraw consent at any time without affecting prior processing.
section7.exercise: To exercise your rights, email privacy@lumifin.io with your full name and the right you wish to exercise. We will respond within 30 days (extendable by 60 days for complex requests, with notice). We may ask for identity verification before fulfilling your request.
section7.transfi: For data held by Transfi as independent controller, please also contact Transfi directly at privacy@transfi.com.
section7.cnil: If you are unsatisfied with our response, you may lodge a complaint with the CNIL (Commission Nationale de l'Informatique et des Libertés) at <1>https://www.cnil.fr</1> or with your local supervisory authority.

section8.title: 8. Security
section8.body: We implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect your data, including: encryption in transit (TLS 1.2+) and at rest; access controls and least-privilege principles; secure authentication (mPIN, biometrics); regular security assessments; incident response procedures.
section8.outro: No system is perfectly secure. If a data breach occurs that poses a high risk to your rights, we will notify you and the relevant supervisory authority as required by Articles 33-34 GDPR.

section9.title: 9. Children
section9.body: The App is not intended for individuals under 18. We do not knowingly collect data from minors. If we discover that a minor has created an Account, we will close it and delete the data promptly.

section10.title: 10. Cookies and Tracking
section10.body: The Lumi App does not use cookies (it is a mobile application). We use Firebase Analytics and Firebase Crashlytics SDKs for usage analytics and crash reporting. You can opt out of analytics collection in the App settings. Our website (lumifin.io) uses only strictly necessary cookies that do not require consent.

section11.body: We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time. Material changes will be notified via the App or email at least 30 days before they take effect. The "Last Updated" date at the top indicates the current version. Continued use of the App after the effective date constitutes acceptance of the updated policy.

q1.question: What is Lumi?
q1.answer: Lumi is a digital wallet that lets you pay at local merchants across Southeast Asia using QR codes. You can pay in your own currency while Lumi handles the conversion instantly at checkout.

q2.question: Which countries can I pay in with Lumi?
q2.answer: Lumi is launching in Vietnam, where you can pay any VietQR code — street stalls, cafés, markets and shops. Thailand (PromptPay) and Indonesia (QRIS) are next, with more of Southeast Asia to follow.

q3.question: How do I pay with Lumi?
q3.answer: Simply open the app, scan the merchant's QR code, enter the amount if required, and confirm the payment using your secure mPIN or biometric authentication.

q4.question: Do I need to convert currency before paying?
q4.answer: No. Lumi automatically converts your payment into the local currency in real time, so you can pay seamlessly without any manual conversion.

q5.question: What exchange rate does Lumi use?
q5.answer: Lumi shows you the live exchange rate and final amount before you confirm your payment, so you always know exactly what you're paying.

q6.question: Are there any fees?
q6.answer: Lumi is transparent about pricing. Any applicable fees, including currency conversion and payment processing fees, are clearly displayed before you complete a transaction.

q7.question: How do I add money to my Lumi wallet?
q7.answer: You can add funds through supported payment methods directly within the app. Credit transfers and direct connections with European bank accounts are supported. The process is simple and most deposits are completed instantly.

q8.question: How long do payments take?
q8.answer: Payments are processed in seconds once confirmed, provided you have an active internet connection. You and the merchant receive the payment confirmation in real time.

q9.question: Is Lumi secure?
q9.answer: Yes. Lumi uses industry-standard security measures, including encryption, identity verification, and secure authentication methods like mPIN and biometrics to protect your account.

q10.question: Why do I need to verify my identity?
q10.answer: Identity verification helps keep your account secure and allows Lumi to comply with financial regulations, ensuring a safe and reliable payment experience.

q11.question: What documents are required for verification?
q11.answer: You'll need to provide a valid government-issued ID, such as a passport or national ID card. In some cases, a selfie may be required for verification.

q12.question: Can I withdraw money from my Lumi wallet?
q12.answer: Yes. You can withdraw funds to a supported bank account or payment method, depending on your location.

q13.question: How long do withdrawals take?
q13.answer: Withdrawal times vary based on the method used, ranging from a few minutes to a few business days.

q14.question: Can I see my transaction history?
q14.answer: Yes. All your payments and transactions are available immediately in the app, so you can track your spending anytime.

q15.question: What happens if I make a wrong payment?
q15.answer: Payments are usually processed instantly and cannot be reversed automatically. If you encounter an issue, you can contact the merchant or Lumi support for assistance.

q16.question: How is my money safeguarded?
q16.answer: Your money is always handled by regulated banking and payment partners — never held directly by Lumi. We work with trusted, licensed institutions across Europe and Asia that follow strict regulatory standards to ensure your funds are protected at every step.

q17.question: Is Lumi a bank?
q17.answer: No, Lumi is not a bank. Lumi is a brand of Lumifin SAS, a technology provider. All payment services and fund movements are carried out by fully regulated partners in Europe and Asia, who are licensed and supervised by financial authorities.

q18.question: Who can sign up for Lumi?
q18.answer: Lumi is currently open to EU and EEA residents with a SEPA bank account in their own name. That covers 30 countries: Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Liechtenstein, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, and Sweden. The UK and Switzerland are not on this list and aren't supported yet, even though they're geographically close to Europe.

q19.question: Can I top up with a credit or debit card?
q19.answer: Not yet. Right now, Lumi works with SEPA transfer or open banking from a European bank account. Credit and debit card top-ups are coming soon.

q20.question: Can tourists use Wise to scan PromptPay QR codes in Thailand?
q20.answer: As of May 2026, Wise's Thai entity offers PromptPay scan-and-pay — but only for customers resident in Thailand, not for EU travellers using their home account. So for a European visitor on a trip, this doesn't help. Lumi is built specifically for EU-resident travellers: top up from your European bank account and scan PromptPay, VietQR or QRIS wherever you go.

q21.question: Is there a minimum amount when I add money?
q21.answer: Yes. The minimum top-up is €25. There is no maximum beyond the limits set during verification, and you can top up as often as you like. If you are not sure how much to load, €25 covers a comfortable day in Vietnam — a room, meals, transport and a paid sight — so it is a sensible starting point for a short trip.

seo.title: Cash Is King? The Real Problems with Carrying Cash in Thailand, Vietnam, and Indonesia
seo.description: Exchange rate traps, ATM fees, pickpocketing risks — the hidden costs of carrying cash in Southeast Asia that nobody warns you about.

cashIsKing.title: Cash Is King? The Real Problems with Carrying Cash in Thailand, Vietnam, and Indonesia
cashIsKing.subtitle: Everyone told me to bring cash. Here's what they didn't tell me.
cashIsKing.author: Lumi Blog
cashIsKing.imgAlt: Cash vs QR payments in Southeast Asia
cashIsKing.p1: You land in Bangkok. It's 11pm, you're jet-lagged, the airport is loud, and somewhere between baggage claim and the exit, you start panicking about cash.
cashIsKing.p2: How much do I need? Should I exchange here or wait? Is the ATM going to swallow my card? Is this enough for the week?
cashIsKing.p3: Almost every first-time traveller to Southeast Asia goes through this exact loop. And almost every seasoned travel forum, blog post, and well-meaning friend has the same advice: bring cash. Lots of it. Cash is king out there.
cashIsKing.p4: Here's the thing — that advice made sense fifteen years ago. I'm not sure it does anymore. And after spending real time in Thailand, Vietnam, and Indonesia, I started noticing just how much friction, risk, and money that old habit was quietly costing me.
cashIsKing.h1: The moment you realise cash has a cost
cashIsKing.p5: My first night in Ho Chi Minh City, I changed $200 at the airport. The rate was bad — I knew it was bad — but I was tired and I just wanted to move. Later I found out I'd lost the equivalent of about $18 in that one transaction. Not a disaster. But not nothing either.
cashIsKing.p6: Over the next few days, I hit an ATM twice because I underestimated how much I'd spend. Each withdrawal came with a flat fee from the local bank, plus whatever my home bank charged on top, plus a currency conversion margin buried somewhere in the small print. By the time I did the maths at the end of the trip, I'd paid somewhere north of €10, just in fees to access my own money.
cashIsKing.p7: Nobody really talks about this part. The "cash is king" advice doesn't come with a footnote that says: also, getting that cash will cost you more than you think, every single time.
cashIsKing.p8: If you've ever stood in front of three different currency exchange booths at a Thai airport and tried to figure out which one is actually giving you the best deal — you know the feeling. The numbers are big (you're dealing in thousands of baht), which makes it hard to eyeball whether you're getting a good rate or a terrible one.
cashIsKing.p9: Airport exchanges are almost always the worst option. Everyone knows this in theory, but when you've just landed and you need baht or dong or rupiah right now, the booths right there are extremely convenient. So you take the hit.
cashIsKing.p10: The local exchanges in tourist areas are better, but "better" is relative. And even the ones that advertise no commission often make it back through a slightly worse rate. ATMs give you something close to the real interbank rate, but then add their own fees on top. There is no clean option. Every path has a cost, and most of them are intentionally difficult to compare.
cashIsKing.p11: You spend so much energy trying to lose as little money as possible that you forget you're supposed to be on holiday.
cashIsKing.h3: The stuff nobody warns you about
cashIsKing.p12: Losing cash is forever. That sounds obvious, but it hits differently when it happens. A friend of mine had her purse lifted on Khao San Road — just the cash, gone. No dispute to file, no chargeback, no fraud protection. Just gone. She spent the next two days figuring out how to get more money while also trying not to let it ruin her trip. And even when you're not out in the crowd, the risk doesn't really go away.
cashIsKing.p13: Keeping cash in your hotel room isn't as safe as it sounds. Unless you're staying in a high-end property, there's always a lingering doubt — what if something goes missing from your luggage? It's not theoretical. I've had friends this has happened to.
cashIsKing.p14: Pickpocketing is real in high-tourist areas across all three countries. Night markets, busy street food spots, tuk-tuks, crowded temples — these are the places you most want to be. And it gets worse at night.
cashIsKing.p15: Imagine being on a walking street — crowded, loud, packed with people — and suddenly needing cash. Pulling out your wallet in that moment doesn't just feel inconvenient, it feels risky. These are exactly the environments where pickpocketing is most common, and they're also exactly where carrying a thick wad of cash becomes a liability. The anxiety of it is low-grade but constant. Where's my wallet? Did I just feel something? How much cash do I have left?
cashIsKing.p16: There's also the ATM problem that no one really prepares you for: the machines aren't always working. Or they're simply out of cash. Or they have withdrawal limits so low that you need to do two or three separate transactions just to get enough for a few days. In smaller towns in Vietnam or the outer islands of Indonesia, finding a working ATM at all can eat up a real chunk of your afternoon.
cashIsKing.p17: Then there's just the daily friction of it.
cashIsKing.p18: Counting out unfamiliar notes while a line of people waits behind you. Handing over what you think is the right amount and having no idea if the change you get back is correct. Trying to break a large bill at a small street stall and watching the vendor's face fall because they don't have change and now neither of you knows what to do.
cashIsKing.p19: In Vietnam especially, the numbers are enormous — you're dealing in millions of dong for everyday transactions. It sounds exciting until you're at a café trying to remember whether 85,000 is less than one dollar or more, while someone waits for you to pay.
cashIsKing.p20: And every few days, you have to do the whole thing again. Find an ATM. Hope it works. Pay the fees. Count the notes. Start over.
cashIsKing.h5: What's actually happening on the ground
cashIsKing.p21: Here's the part that surprised me most: the locals aren't doing any of this.
cashIsKing.p22: In Bangkok's weekend markets, vendors have QR codes taped to their stalls. At street food spots in Hanoi, the lady running the pho cart holds up her phone and the person in front of me scans and pays without breaking stride. In Bali, the family-run warung down the road from my guesthouse had a QRIS code on the counter and most of their regulars just used it without thinking.
cashIsKing.p23: Thailand's PromptPay, Vietnam's VietQR, Indonesia's QRIS — these systems exist, they work, and they're used millions of times a day. The infrastructure for a cashless transaction is already there. The locals figured this out. The tourist advice just hasn't caught up yet.
cashIsKing.p24: The "cash is king" belief persists partly because it used to be true, and partly because old travel advice is very sticky. But the ground reality in these three countries has shifted significantly in the last few years, and it's still shifting. Walking around with a wallet full of local currency is starting to feel less like a safety net and more like a habit that doesn't quite fit anymore.
cashIsKing.p25: The honest answer is: it depends on where you're going and what you're doing. Deep rural areas still run on cash. Some older vendors won't have a QR code. You'll probably still need some local currency in your pocket, especially for smaller towns and more remote spots.
cashIsKing.p26: But the idea that you need to arrive with a fat envelope of cash, budget for exchange fees, hunt for ATMs, and carry the constant low-level stress of losing it all? That's becoming less true with every trip. Mobile payments — particularly QR-based ones — are safer because there's nothing physical to lose or steal. They're more transparent because you can see exactly what you paid and in what currency. And they're fast in a way that fumbling with unfamiliar notes simply isn't.
cashIsKing.p27: The question isn't really "cash or no cash." It's whether you want to keep absorbing all the hidden costs — the fees, the bad rates, the risk, the hassle — out of habit, or start travelling a little smarter.
cashIsKing.blockquote: Cash isn't king anymore. It's just familiar. And familiar isn't always the same thing as safe.
cashIsKing.p28: That's exactly why we're building Lumi — to remove the friction from how money moves across borders.
cashIsKing.closing: Because paying for something, anywhere in the world, shouldn't be this hard.

seo.title: QRIS Decoded — Indonesia's QR Payment System for European Travelers

qrisDecoded.title: QRIS Decoded: Indonesia's Standardized QR Payment System and What It Means for European Travelers
qrisDecoded.subtitle: With over 56 million merchants and 6 billion transactions, QRIS is how Indonesia pays. And as a European visitor, you're currently locked out of it.
qrisDecoded.author: Lumi
qrisDecoded.imgAlt: QRIS QR Payment System in Indonesia
qrisDecoded.p1: Picture this: you're at a warung in Ubud, Bali. You've just had the best nasi goreng of your life and the bill comes to 45,000 IDR — roughly €2.50. You reach for your European bank card, and the vendor points to a small printed QR code on the counter. No card terminal. No cash preferred. Just a QR code. And you have absolutely no way to scan it.
qrisDecoded.p2: Welcome to QRIS — pronounced "quris" — Indonesia's national QR payment standard that has quietly become the backbone of everyday commerce across the archipelago. With over 56 million registered merchants and 6 billion transactions in just the first half of 2025, QRIS isn't a niche experiment. It's how Indonesia pays.
qrisDecoded.h1: And as a European visitor, you're currently locked out of it.
qrisDecoded.p3: QRIS stands for Quick Response Code Indonesian Standard. Launched by Bank Indonesia in 2019, it was designed to solve a very real problem: Indonesia's digital payment market was fragmented across dozens of competing e-wallets — GoPay, OVO, Dana, ShopeePay, LinkAja — each with its own QR code. A merchant would need to display five or six different QR codes, and customers could only pay with the one matching their app.
qrisDecoded.p4: QRIS unified all of this into a single standard. One QR code, any compatible wallet or bank app. The merchant displays one code; the customer scans it with whichever payment app they prefer. Simple, instant, and with zero transaction fees for micro-merchants.
qrisDecoded.tableIntro: To understand why QRIS matters, consider the numbers:
qrisDecoded.tableRow2Desc: Of which are MSMEs (micro, small & medium enterprises)
qrisDecoded.tableRow5Desc: QRIS Tap (NFC) users since March 2025 launch
qrisDecoded.p5: In practical terms, QRIS is accepted everywhere from Jakarta's modern malls to the smallest street-side kaki lima food cart in Yogyakarta. In March 2025, Bank Indonesia also launched QRIS Tap — an NFC-based contactless version — which already reached 47.8 million users within months of launch.
qrisDecoded.h4: Why European tourists are locked out
qrisDecoded.p6: Here's the catch. QRIS was built for Indonesia's domestic banking and e-wallet infrastructure. To use it, you need either a local Indonesian bank account (which requires a KITAS residence permit) or a local e-wallet like GoPay or OVO (which requires an Indonesian phone number and, for full functionality, local ID verification).
qrisDecoded.p7: As a European tourist or even a long-stay digital nomad on a visitor visa, you can't access any of these. So you're left with three unappealing options:
qrisDecoded.option1Bold: Pay with your European debit or credit card
qrisDecoded.option1Rest: — where it's accepted, which is mostly limited to hotels, upscale restaurants, and tourist-oriented businesses. Expect 1.5–3% foreign transaction fees plus unfavorable exchange rates.
qrisDecoded.option2Rest: — Indonesian ATMs typically charge 30,000–50,000 IDR per withdrawal (€1.70–€2.80), with limits of 1,250,000–2,500,000 IDR per transaction. Your European bank adds its own fees on top. Carrying large amounts of cash also comes with security risks.
qrisDecoded.option3Rest: — which means dealing with variable rates, potential scams (especially in tourist areas like Kuta), and the inconvenience of always having the right denomination.
qrisDecoded.p8: Meanwhile, the Indonesian person next to you scans a QR code, pays instantly, and walks away. The transaction cost them nothing extra. The merchant got the money in seconds.
qrisDecoded.h5: Cross-border QRIS: progress, but not for Europe (yet)
qrisDecoded.p9: Bank Indonesia has been actively expanding QRIS internationally — but primarily within Asia. Through the ASEAN cross-border payment linkage initiative, QRIS now connects with Thailand's PromptPay, Malaysia's DuitNow, Singapore's PayNow, and several other regional systems. In August 2025, QRIS launched in Japan, and South Korea is joining in April 2026.
qrisDecoded.p10: This means a Thai tourist in Bali can scan a QRIS code and pay with their Thai banking app. A Singaporean can do the same. But a French, German, or Dutch traveler? No pathway exists — yet.
qrisDecoded.blockquote1: This is precisely the gap that solutions like Lumi are designed to bridge.
qrisDecoded.p11: Giving European travelers access to local QR payment infrastructure without needing a local bank account or e-wallet.
qrisDecoded.h6: What this means for your next trip to Indonesia
qrisDecoded.p12: If you're planning to visit Indonesia — whether for a two-week holiday in Bali, a month of remote work in Canggu, or a business trip to Jakarta — understanding QRIS is essential. It's not a payment "option" in Indonesia; it's increasingly the default. Many smaller merchants, transport services, and even market vendors now prefer or exclusively accept QRIS over cash.
qrisDecoded.p13: The good news: the infrastructure is mature, secure, and regulated by Bank Indonesia. The technology works flawlessly. The only missing piece is access for international visitors from outside Asia.
qrisDecoded.blockquote2: And that's exactly what we're working on at Lumi. Stay tuned.

seo.title: Why We Built Lumi — A Founder's Story
seo.description: The two moments that changed everything: a cab ride in Kuala Lumpur and an artist in Northern Thailand. The real story behind Lumi.

whyWeBuiltLumi.titleAfter: — and the two moments I can't stop thinking about
whyWeBuiltLumi.subtitle: This isn't a polished origin story. It's just what actually happened.
whyWeBuiltLumi.author: Lumi Founder
whyWeBuiltLumi.p1: I left my wallet at hotel during a trip to Malaysia.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p2: Not a big deal, I thought. I never really use it anyway. I live on my phone — everything's on there. I'd be fine.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p3: Later, I took a cab from my hotel to a restaurant.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p4: The cab pulled up outside the restaurant. The driver turned around and waited. I reached into my pocket for my wallet and — nothing. Just my phone.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p5: No worries, I thought. I'll pay on my phone somehow. But I didn't have any local payment app set up. My credit card wasn't linked to anything he could accept. He started showing me his QR code. Again. And again. Each time a little more frustrated, a little more resigned.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p6: I just stood there. Phone in hand. Money in my account. And absolutely no way to pay the man standing right in front of me.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p7: The shame of that moment was something specific. It wasn't the embarrassment of forgetting something — that happens to everyone. It was the feeling of being completely helpless in a situation that should not exist. I had a smartphone. I had money. The technology existed. And yet, somehow, none of it could close a ten-foot gap between me and a cab driver who just wanted to get paid for his work.
whyWeBuiltLumi.blockquote1: I had everything I needed — except the one thing that actually mattered in that moment.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p8: We sorted it eventually. Someone nearby stepped in to help. But I sat in my room that night and couldn't let it go. I started thinking about the real cost of how we move money across borders.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p9: Credit cards? Over 5% in total fees once you add up the foreign transaction charge, the currency conversion markup, and whatever your bank quietly takes. And that's when the merchant even has a card machine — which, in huge parts of the world, they simply don't.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p10: Cash? I always end up carrying three currencies "just in case," worrying about losing it, and coming home with a pile of useless leftover notes I'll never use again.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p11: Neither option was actually working. They were just the options we'd all quietly accepted.
whyWeBuiltLumi.location2: 📍 Northern Thailand, A Few Days Later
whyWeBuiltLumi.p12: I was walking through a small town — not a tourist spot, just a real place — when I saw an older woman sitting on the roadside with the most beautiful handmade artwork laid out around her. Intricate, colourful pieces that clearly took real skill and real time.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p13: I stopped. I wanted to buy something.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p14: She looked up and smiled, and in careful, broken English she pointed to a QR code she'd printed out and laminated. She'd clearly done this before — prepared for this exact situation, hoping for this exact customer.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p15: I only had euros on me. Not thai baht, not a working QR payment setup, nothing she could use. I tried to explain. She kept pointing at the code, switching between Thai and fragments of English, not understanding why this wasn't working. And then, slowly, she seemed to understand.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p16: She picked up one of her paintings and held it out to me.
whyWeBuiltLumi.blockquote2Line2: There were tears in her eyes.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p17: I couldn't take it. I shook my head, said thank you, and walked away. Not because I didn't want it — I wanted it more than anything in that market. But because she needed to sell it, not give it away to some tourist who couldn't figure out how to pay her.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p18: That walk away was the moment everything became clear to me.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p19: She had prepared everything she could. A QR code. A smile. Hope. And the global payments system still failed her.
whyWeBuiltLumi.h3: That's when we decided to build something.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p20: The technology to fix this already exists. QR payments, digital wallets, interoperable systems — none of this is new. What's missing is something that brings it together in a way that actually works for the cab driver in KL and the artist on a roadside in Thailand, not just for people who are already plugged into the right apps and banks.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p21: That's what Lumi is trying to be.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p22: Not another fintech product for people who already have everything. Something genuinely more inclusive — that works whether you're the one travelling or the one waiting for a customer, whether you have a card machine or a laminated QR code, whether you're in a major city or a small town that the formal banking system forgot about.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p23: I think about that woman a lot. I don't know her name. I never got the painting. But every decision we make building Lumi, I ask myself the same question: would this have helped her?
whyWeBuiltLumi.blockquote3: If the answer is no, we're not done yet.
whyWeBuiltLumi.p24: If you've ever been stuck on the wrong side of a broken payment — as a customer or a seller — I'd genuinely love to hear about it.

seo.title: Vietnam Skipped the Card Era — VietQR Explained for Travellers
seo.description: Why your Mastercard fails at a Hanoi café, and the four payment systems running daily life in Vietnam: VietQR, MoMo, ZaloPay, VNPay.

vietqrDecoded.title: Vietnam Skipped the Card Era. Your Mastercard Didn’t Get the Memo.
vietqrDecoded.subtitle: VietQR explained — and why foreigners can’t use the apps that run daily life in Vietnam.
vietqrDecoded.author: Gaurav Bansal
vietqrDecoded.imgAlt: A street vendor in Vietnam accepting a VietQR payment
vietqrDecoded.h1: A Hanoi café, three failed taps
vietqrDecoded.p1: Almost no one in Vietnam carries a wallet anymore. They carry a phone. They scan a QR code, hear a small beep from the merchant’s speaker, and it’s done. A bánh mì paid for in three seconds.
vietqrDecoded.p2: Meanwhile, your Premium Mastercard sits useless in your back pocket at a Hanoi café. The waiter has tried the card machine twice. The guy at the next table just paid for his iced coffee with a glance at his phone.
vietqrDecoded.p3: This is the story of how Vietnam built a payment system that quietly works better than ours. And why your bank still hasn’t figured out how to talk to it.
vietqrDecoded.p4: Fifteen years ago, Vietnam ran on cash. About 99% of retail in 2010 was paper money.
vietqrDecoded.p5: Today is different. The State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) says non-cash payments grew more than 50% in 2024 by transaction count. QR payments alone more than doubled. MoMo, the most popular wallet, has passed 31 million users. That’s roughly half the adult population. Walk through a wet market in Hanoi and you’ll see grandmothers selling vegetables with a QR code propped against a cucumber.
vietqrDecoded.p6: For comparison: China took about ten years to make the switch to mobile money. India did it in five with UPI. Vietnam did it in around six, without a Tencent and without a government push as forceful as India’s. The country built a shared QR rail (VietQR) and let four local apps fight over the rest. The fight is still going. That’s part of why it works.
vietqrDecoded.p7: People often think Vietnamese payments are one app. They’re not. There are four players, each doing a different job.
vietqrDecoded.sys1Rest: is the rails. It’s not an app you download. It’s a shared QR format that any Vietnamese bank or wallet can read. NAPAS launched it in 2021. It’s why a Vietcombank customer can pay a Techcombank merchant by pointing a phone at a piece of paper. In daily life: that A4 sheet taped to the wall of the cơm tấm shop, with the owner’s account number on it.
vietqrDecoded.sys2Rest: is the consumer wallet. It started as a phone top-up app and grew into Vietnam’s version of WeChat Pay. Bills, food delivery, ride payments, gold, lottery tickets — all in one app. In daily life: paying back a friend who covered last weekend’s Grab. You don’t open your bank app for that. You open MoMo.
vietqrDecoded.sys3Rest: sits on top of Zalo, the messaging app that beat WhatsApp in Vietnam years ago. You use it when paying is part of a conversation. A school parents’ group collecting class-trip money. A Zalo seller posting a dress for sale. In daily life: a Tết red envelope dropped into a group chat.
vietqrDecoded.sys4Rest: is the bank-and-merchant network. Less flashy. More everywhere. It powers most retail point-of-sale across supermarkets, utility bills, airlines, and government services. If MoMo is the wallet in your hand, VNPay is the plumbing behind the “Pay by QR” button in your bank app. In daily life: paying your electricity bill by scanning the code on the invoice.
vietqrDecoded.p8: So: VietQR is the language, the three apps are dialects, and they all work with each other. No one in Vietnam thinks about which logo is on the sticker.
vietqrDecoded.p9: It’s not really a tech story. It’s a money story.
vietqrDecoded.p10: A Vietnamese café that takes Visa or Mastercard pays around 3% per swipe once you add up issuer, scheme, acquirer, and FX fees. A café that takes VietQR pays close to nothing. Usually under 0.3%, often zero. NAPAS keeps the cost low, and most banks throw in free QR for merchants to win their business.
vietqrDecoded.p11: On a 50,000 đồng iced coffee, the difference is small. On a 5-million đồng dinner bill, it’s a day of staff pay. Across a month of dinners, it’s rent.
vietqrDecoded.p12: This is why even cafés in District 1 that call themselves “international friendly” quietly prefer you scan. The card machine is there for the foreigner who insists. It’s not the rail they would choose. Starbucks and McDonald’s still take cards because their parent companies have global card deals. Walk three doors down and the math flips.
vietqrDecoded.p13: Vietnam didn’t push Visa out. Visa just never won the merchant fight. The country jumped straight from cash to QR. It skipped the years where shops bought card terminals and ate the 3% fee as a cost of doing business. There was no installed base of card machines to defend. So the cheaper rail won by default.
vietqrDecoded.p14: You can stand in a Vinmart, watch the local in front of you pay in under two seconds with MoMo, and want very much to do the same thing. You won’t be able to. Here’s why.
vietqrDecoded.p15: To open a MoMo, ZaloPay, or any local wallet, you need three things. All of them have to be issued in Vietnam.
vietqrDecoded.req1Rest: — the chip card called CCCD gắn chip. For foreigners, a long-term residence card works. A tourist visa stamp does not. The app checks your ID against the government database and rejects passports that aren’t linked.
vietqrDecoded.req2Rest: tied to the same ID. Since the 2023 SIM clean-up, every active number is supposed to be registered to a verified national ID. Tourist SIMs don’t pass wallet checks.
vietqrDecoded.req3Rest: . That itself means walking into a branch with your passport, valid visa, proof of address, and usually a work permit or residence card. Neobanks like Cake, Timo, and TNEX have lighter sign-up flows. But they still ask for the same paperwork.
vietqrDecoded.p16: The wall isn’t an accident. It’s how Vietnam follows anti-money-laundering rules and keeps wallet fraud low. Compared to the Philippines or Indonesia, fraud cases per million users in Vietnamese wallets are noticeably lower, and the strict KYC is a big reason why.
vietqrDecoded.p17: The cost is real, though. If you’re a tourist, a digital nomad on a 90-day visa, or a business traveler in for a week, the local payment system is closed to you. Not unfriendly — just closed.
vietqrDecoded.p18: A few honest workarounds, in order of usefulness.
vietqrDecoded.workWiseRest: Wise can send VND straight into a Vietnamese bank account. But you still need an account on the other end. Useful for one-off payments — a landlord, a contractor. Not for daily life. Trade-off: you need a Vietnamese person to receive it.
vietqrDecoded.workMomoRest: The most common move for long-stay foreigners. Hand a friend cash. They MoMo it where you need it to go. Trade-off: awkward above $100 and impossible to scale.
vietqrDecoded.workEcomRest: Shopee, Lazada, and Grab take international Visa and Mastercard directly. You can order food, ride, and shop without ever touching VietQR. Trade-off: doesn’t help at the bánh mì cart.
vietqrDecoded.workHotelRest: Mid-range hotels and up will often charge MoMo top-ups, Grab credits, or bills to your room. They pay in VND. You pay them with your card at checkout. Trade-off: small spread.
vietqrDecoded.p19: And bring cash. ATMs are everywhere and the exchange rate is fine. Notes of 500,000 đồng are useful for hotels and taxis; smaller notes are useful for almost everything else. Avoid changing money at the airport — the rate at any bank in town is better, and the gold shops on Hà Trung in Hanoi are better still.
vietqrDecoded.p20: The wall is starting to crack. In early 2026, the SBV confirmed the next step in the ASEAN cross-border QR link. Vietnamese travellers can already scan Thai PromptPay codes with their bank apps. Thai visitors scanning Vietnamese QRs went live in pilot cities late last year. A Singapore–Vietnam link with PayNow is being built. Cambodia is reportedly next.
vietqrDecoded.p21: What this doesn’t fix is the foreigner problem from the other direction — a French traveller scanning a VietQR with a French bank app. That’s the harder one. It needs interbank settlement with non-ASEAN systems, and European and American banks don’t have a commercial reason to bother yet. SBV officials have said they’re “open to” wider foreign access. They haven’t put a date on it.
vietqrDecoded.p22: The honest forecast: by the end of 2026, anyone with a Thai, Singaporean, Malaysian, Indonesian, or Cambodian bank app will be able to pay at a Vietnamese street stall. Everyone else still queues at the ATM. If you’re reading this from London, New York, or Berlin, plan accordingly.
vietqrDecoded.lumiTip: This is the kind of fragmentation we’re working to smooth out. A single layer over local rails, so travellers and remote teams can pay in Vietnam without the KYC headache.
vietqrDecoded.p23: If you move money in and out of Vietnam often, we have a quieter path than handing your friend a stack of cash. Before your next trip:
vietqrDecoded.tip1: Tell your card company you’re travelling so they don’t block you.
vietqrDecoded.tip2: Bring at least 3 million đồng in cash for the first two days.
vietqrDecoded.tip3: Install Grab and Shopee before you land. Both take foreign cards.
vietqrDecoded.tip4: Staying more than 30 days? Ask your hotel about MoMo top-ups in their name. Most will do it.

seo.title: Best Travel Cards for Europeans in Vietnam (2026 Comparison)
seo.description: Compare Wise, Revolut, N26, Monzo, cash and Lumi for paying in Vietnam as a European traveller in 2026 — and the smartest payment setup to bring.

bestTravelCardsVietnam.title: Best Travel Cards for Europeans in Vietnam (2026 Comparison)
bestTravelCardsVietnam.subtitle: Wise, Revolut, N26, Monzo and traditional bank cards can all help in Vietnam — but none of them fully solves the local QR payment problem. Here's the practical setup Europeans should bring in 2026.
bestTravelCardsVietnam.author: Thiofanty
bestTravelCardsVietnam.imgAlt: European traveller paying by QR code at a cafe in Vietnam with a smartphone.
bestTravelCardsVietnam.shortAnswerP1: If you're travelling to Vietnam from Europe in 2026, the smartest payment setup isn't one perfect card. It's a stack: one low-fee travel card, one backup bank card, some cash for edge cases, and a QR-ready option for everyday local payments.
bestTravelCardsVietnam.shortAnswerP2: Wise, Revolut, N26 and Monzo are all useful because they usually give better foreign spending experiences than old-school bank cards. But in Vietnam, the bigger problem isn't only exchange rates. It's access. Many everyday merchants are set up for local QR payments, not foreign cards.

Weekend / plan / fair-use fees can apply
