tableRows.watchOut: ATM withdrawals in foreign currency may cost extra on free plans
FX markups, ATM fees and blocks

tableRows.bestFor: Paying by local QR from a European account

bestTravelCardsVietnam.howPayH: How people actually pay in Vietnam
bestTravelCardsVietnam.howPayP1: Vietnam isn't a "card-first" travel market in the way many Europeans expect. In hotels, malls, airports, tourist restaurants and larger stores, Visa and Mastercard are usually useful. But for small cafes, street food, local shops, taxis, market vendors and casual services, you'll often see a QR code on the counter before you see a card terminal.
bestTravelCardsVietnam.howPayP2: This isn't just a vibe. Vietnam's non-cash payment growth has been fast. In the first 11 months of 2024, non-cash payment transaction volume rose 56.8% year on year, and QR code payments grew 106.7% by volume, according to State Bank of Vietnam figures reported by Vietnam News. [7]
bestTravelCardsVietnam.howPayP3: The system behind a lot of this is VietQR, a common QR standard launched through the NAPAS network and member banks. For locals, the experience is simple: open a banking app, scan the merchant QR code, confirm the amount, and the payment moves in VND. For visitors, the interface is visible everywhere, but access is less straightforward. [8]
bestTravelCardsVietnam.bringH: So, what should Europeans actually bring?
bestTravelCardsVietnam.bringIntro: Bring at least two cards and don't make cash your only plan. A good first setup looks like this:
bringList: One low-fee travel card such as Wise, Revolut, N26 or Monzo.
One traditional bank card as a backup in case your main card is blocked.
Some VND cash for arrival, street food, rural areas and emergencies.
A QR-ready option if you want to pay like locals in daily merchant settings.

cards.name: Wise in Vietnam
cards.p1: Wise is probably the most practical "default" card for many Europeans because it's built around transparent currency conversion and international spending. It works well when a merchant accepts international cards, and it's useful for ATM withdrawals if you stay within your allowance.
cards.p2: The catch is that Wise is still a card-first solution. It helps with the exchange-rate layer, but it doesn't automatically make every local QR code in Vietnam usable. Wise says UK card users get free ATM withdrawals up to a monthly allowance of GBP 250, with a 2.69% fee on amounts above that allowance, and ATM operators may still charge their own fees. [1]
cards.verdictRest: everyday card spending, backup ATM access and travellers who care about transparent FX. Not best for: paying at QR-only places unless the specific merchant flow is supported by a partner integration.

cards.name: Revolut in Vietnam
cards.p1: Revolut is strong for travellers who like managing currencies inside an app. It's convenient, familiar, and useful as a spending card where international cards are accepted. For many Europeans, it's also the card already sitting in Apple Pay or Google Pay before they leave.
cards.p2: The watch-out is that Revolut's fees depend on your country, plan, timing and limits. For example, Revolut France's Standard plan shows free ATM withdrawals up to five withdrawals or EUR 200 per rolling month, then a 2% fee with a EUR 1 minimum. Revolut Netherlands' Standard terms say weekend currency exchange can trigger a 1% fee. [2] [3]
cards.verdictRest: app control, multi-currency spending and travellers who already use Revolut. Not best for: assuming every conversion is free in every situation, or assuming Revolut alone unlocks local QR acceptance.

cards.name: N26 in Vietnam
cards.p1: N26 is clean and simple if your base life is already in euros. Card spending abroad can be convenient, and N26 says it doesn't charge exchange markups on card payments, using the Mastercard exchange rate. That makes it easy to understand for standard card acceptance. [4]
cards.p2: Cash withdrawals are the part to check. N26 says Standard, Business and Smart accounts pay a 1.7% fee on foreign-currency ATM withdrawals, while that fee is waived on Go and Metal plans. Again, local ATM operators may still add their own charges. [5]
cards.verdictRest: euro-based travellers who want simple card spending. Not best for: QR-first local payments, because N26 is still primarily a card account in this context.

cards.name: Monzo in Vietnam
cards.p1: Monzo is most relevant for UK travellers. It's not an EU bank, but many Europeans and UK-based travellers compare it with Wise and Revolut before a Southeast Asia trip. Monzo says card spending abroad is fee-free and uses Mastercard's exchange rate.
cards.p2: For cash outside the EEA, its free withdrawal allowance depends on account type, with a 3% fee after the allowance. [6]
cards.verdictRest: UK travellers who want simple card payments and good app notifications. Not best for: heavy cash use outside the allowance, or unlocking local VietQR by itself.

bestTravelCardsVietnam.tradP1: Your bank card from home is worth bringing, but it shouldn't be your main Vietnam payment strategy unless you've checked the fees. Traditional bank cards can work in larger merchants, but many charge foreign transaction fees, use less attractive exchange rates, or add ATM charges. They can also trigger fraud blocks when you suddenly start tapping in Vietnam.
bestTravelCardsVietnam.tradP2: Best for backup; not for daily spending if your bank adds FX and ATM costs. Before you go, check three things: the foreign transaction fee, the ATM withdrawal fee, and whether dynamic currency conversion is blocked or warned about in-app.
bestTravelCardsVietnam.cashP1: Cash is still useful in Vietnam. You'll want VND for small vendors, tips, rural areas, old-school shops and moments when your phone battery or data connection gives up. The mistake is relying on cash for everything and treating ATM fees or airport exchange as invisible.
bestTravelCardsVietnam.cashP2: Use ATMs when you need them, but withdraw intentionally. Frequent small withdrawals can be expensive because you may pay your card provider's fee, the ATM operator's fee, and a conversion spread. When a terminal or ATM asks whether to charge you in euros or VND, choosing VND is usually the cleaner option because it avoids dynamic currency conversion markups.
bestTravelCardsVietnam.missingH: The missing piece: local QR payments
bestTravelCardsVietnam.missingP1: Here's where the usual "best travel card" advice breaks down. The best card for Vietnam may still fail at the exact moment you want convenience: a QR code at a cafe, a local food counter, a small shop or a service provider who doesn't want to deal with card rails.
bestTravelCardsVietnam.missingP2: Some tourist-facing QR options are emerging. For example, Da Nang's tourism portal describes a VNPAY flow for international visitors that uses an international phone number, passport details and a linked Visa, Mastercard or JCB card. That's useful directionally, but the broader lesson is simpler: Vietnam is moving toward QR, and travellers need payment tools that meet the local flow instead of forcing every purchase back onto cards and cash. [9]
bestTravelCardsVietnam.lumifinP1: Lumi isn't trying to replace your travel card. It's designed to fill the QR gap: helping Europeans pay like locals in Vietnam using local QR payments, without needing a Vietnamese bank account. For now, the simplest stack is still: keep your travel card, carry some cash, and use Lumi when local QR is the better way to pay.
bestTravelCardsVietnam.first24H: Best payment setup for your first 24 hours in Vietnam

first24List.rest: add Wise / Revolut / N26 / Monzo to your phone wallet if you use one, and bring a physical card too.
avoid changing your whole budget at the first exchange counter. Get enough cash for the first day only.
test one card payment in a larger merchant, withdraw a small amount of VND if needed, and keep notes on the fees shown in-app.
expect QR codes in local places. If you can't use them yet, keep cash as a fallback.
pay in VND, not euros, if a terminal offers a choice.

bestTravelCardsVietnam.verdictP1: If you only want the best European travel card for Vietnam, choose Wise or Revolut as your main card, N26 if you want a euro-native bank card, and Monzo if you're UK-based. But if you want the best payment setup, think bigger than cards.
bestTravelCardsVietnam.verdictP2: Vietnam is increasingly QR-first in everyday life. Cards are useful, cash is still necessary, and QR access is becoming the difference between paying like a visitor and paying like someone who actually lives there.
bestTravelCardsVietnam.verdictP3: The smart 2026 setup: one strong travel card, one backup card, a small amount of VND cash, and a QR-ready payment option for everyday local merchants.

seo.title: Digital Nomad Visas in Thailand, Vietnam, and Bali: 2026 Comparison
seo.description: Thailand, Vietnam, and Bali all attract remote workers, but their visa routes are very different. Here is the practical 2026 comparison for Europeans choosing a Southeast Asia base.

digitalNomadVisas.title: Digital Nomad Visas in Thailand, Vietnam, and Bali: The 2026 Comparison
digitalNomadVisas.subtitle: Thailand, Vietnam, and Bali all attract remote workers — but their visa routes are very different. Here's the practical 2026 comparison for Europeans choosing a Southeast Asia base.
digitalNomadVisas.author: Pierre Lahbabi
digitalNomadVisas.imgAlt: A remote worker comparing Thailand, Vietnam, and Bali visa options with a passport, laptop, and coffee on a cafe table.
digitalNomadVisas.introP1: You're choosing between Chiang Mai, Da Nang, and Canggu. The cafes look good. The rent feels possible. The Wi-Fi seems fine. Then you open the visa requirements.
digitalNomadVisas.introP2: That's usually where the dream gets more practical.
digitalNomadVisas.introP3: For European remote workers, Thailand, Vietnam, and Bali are three of the most common Southeast Asia options. They can all work as a base, but they don't offer the same level of visa clarity. Thailand has a clearer remote-work route. Vietnam is flexible for shorter stays, but doesn't currently have a dedicated digital nomad visa. Bali, through Indonesia, has a remote worker visa route, but the paperwork is more serious.
digitalNomadVisas.introP4: This guide compares the 2026 options in plain English, so you can understand what each destination is actually good for before you book the flight. Visa rules change often, so treat this as a decision guide, not legal advice. Always check official immigration sources before applying.
shortAnswerList: Choose Thailand if you want the clearest long-stay route for remote work.
Choose Vietnam if you want a flexible, affordable base for one to three months.
Choose Bali, Indonesia, if you want lifestyle and community, and you have the documentation for a formal remote worker route.
digitalNomadVisas.shortAnswerP: The best destination isn't only the one with the easiest visa. It's the one where your visa, work rhythm, budget, payments, internet, and daily life all fit together.

digitalNomadVisas.comparisonP: The practical difference is simple: Thailand is the most purpose-built for digital nomads, Vietnam is the easiest to test for a shorter stay, and Bali is the strongest lifestyle brand with a more formal Indonesia-based route.
digitalNomadVisas.thailandP1: Thailand is currently the strongest option if you want visa clarity as a remote worker.
digitalNomadVisas.thailandP2: The Destination Thailand Visa, usually called the DTV, is designed for people entering Thailand partly as tourists and partly to work remotely. The official Thai Consulate in Frankfurt describes the DTV Workation route for digital nomads, remote workers, and freelancers. It allows multiple entries, with a maximum stay of 180 days per entry, and has 5-year validity. [1]
digitalNomadVisas.thailandP3: The same official page lists a financial evidence requirement of at least 500,000 THB, about EUR 13,000 at recent exchange rates, plus proof of employment, an employment certificate, or a professional portfolio showing remote worker or freelance status. The listed visa fee through that consulate is EUR 350. [1]
digitalNomadVisas.thailandP4: This doesn't mean every application is automatic. Requirements can vary by embassy or consulate, and immigration officers can request additional documents. But compared with many Southeast Asia options, Thailand gives remote workers a clearer framework.
thailandFit: You want to stay longer than a normal holiday.
You can prove remote work, freelance work, or overseas employment.
You like the idea of moving between Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Phuket, Koh Samui, or Koh Phangan.
You want a mature nomad scene with coworking spaces, cafes, gyms, events, and easy domestic travel.
digitalNomadVisas.thailandClose: Thailand isn't always the lowest-admin choice, but it's the cleanest route if you want to plan beyond a short tourist stay.
digitalNomadVisas.vietnamH: Vietnam: flexible and affordable, but not a digital nomad visa
digitalNomadVisas.vietnamP1: Vietnam is often the easiest country to fall in love with for a few months.
digitalNomadVisas.vietnamP2: Da Nang gives you beach, cafes, coworking spaces, and a slower rhythm. Ho Chi Minh City gives you energy, food, nightlife, and startup density. Hanoi gives you history, culture, and a more northern pace. For many Europeans, Vietnam feels practical because daily life can be affordable, lively, and easy to enjoy quickly.
digitalNomadVisas.vietnamP3: But from a visa perspective, Vietnam isn't the same as Thailand. Vietnam doesn't currently have a dedicated digital nomad visa. Many remote workers rely on the e-visa system or visa exemption rules, depending on passport.
digitalNomadVisas.vietnamP4: Vietnam's official e-visa portal states that the e-visa is valid for a maximum of 90 days and can be single or multiple entry. The official e-visa fee is listed as USD 25 for single entry and USD 50 for multiple entry, about EUR 22 and EUR 43 at recent exchange rates. For a one to three-month stay, that can be enough. For a long-term base, it requires more planning. [2]
vietnamFit: You want to test Southeast Asia without committing to a long visa route.
You're staying for a few weeks to three months.
You care about food, cafes, cost of living, and city energy.
You're comfortable checking visa rules carefully before each stay.
digitalNomadVisas.vietnamClose: Vietnam isn't the strongest option for formal digital nomad visa clarity. It's strong because it's easy to try, easy to like, and easy to build a daily routine around for a shorter stay.
digitalNomadVisas.baliH: Bali, Indonesia: lifestyle first, paperwork second
digitalNomadVisas.baliP1: People say "Bali digital nomad visa," but technically Bali doesn't issue visas. Bali is part of Indonesia. So the relevant route is Indonesian immigration, especially the E33G Remote Worker Visa, sometimes described as a remote worker ITAS route.
digitalNomadVisas.baliP2: Indonesia's official immigration page for E33G says the visa allows you to stay in Indonesia to carry out duties from a company outside Indonesia. It lists a 1-year stay, no sponsor requirement, and application through the eVisa system. The official fee breakdown totals 7,000,000 IDR for a 1-year stay, about EUR 370 at recent exchange rates. [3]
digitalNomadVisas.baliP3: The special requirements are more demanding than Vietnam's e-visa. The official page lists bank evidence showing salary or income of at least USD 60,000 per year, plus an employment agreement with a company established outside Indonesia. [3]
digitalNomadVisas.baliP4: That makes Bali attractive, but not casual. It's best for remote workers who already have stable overseas employment, a clear income trail, and the patience to prepare documentation.
baliFit: You want the Bali lifestyle: Canggu, Pererenan, Ubud, Uluwatu, surf, wellness, and community.
You have stable overseas income and employment documentation.
You're staying longer and want a more formal route than a tourist stay.
You're comfortable with higher living costs in the most popular areas.
digitalNomadVisas.baliClose: Bali can be beautiful, social, and productive. But the visa route isn't just a vibe. It needs proper documents.
digitalNomadVisas.rhythmH: Choose based on your work rhythm, not only the visa
digitalNomadVisas.rhythmP1: A visa is the entry ticket. It doesn't decide whether your month actually works.
digitalNomadVisas.rhythmP2: If you have client calls every day, you may care more about time zones, internet stability, and apartment setup than beach access. If you're freelancing between projects, you may want cheaper living costs and flexible movement. If you're building a company, you may want a stronger founder or operator network.
digitalNomadVisas.rhythmStabilityP: Thailand is the strongest first look. The DTV gives you a more structured remote-work path, and cities like Bangkok and Chiang Mai make it easier to build routines.
digitalNomadVisas.rhythmFlexP: Vietnam is a good first test. You can spend one to three months in Da Nang, Ho Chi Minh City, or Hanoi, learn how you work there, and decide later whether you want something longer-term.
digitalNomadVisas.rhythmLifestyleH: If you want lifestyle and community
digitalNomadVisas.rhythmLifestyleP: Bali is hard to ignore. The community is mature, the lifestyle is strong, and the remote-work culture is visible everywhere. Just make sure the visa route matches your employment and income situation.

dailyRows.thailand: Strongest of the three for remote work
dailyRows.vietnam: Flexible for shorter stays, but no dedicated nomad visa
dailyRows.bali: Formal remote worker route, but more demanding

dailyRows.thailand: Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Phuket, Koh Samui
dailyRows.vietnam: Da Nang, Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi, Hoi An
Often lower, especially outside HCMC/Hanoi expat zones
dailyRows.bali: Can be high in popular areas
Very mature creator and nomad scene

dailyRows.vietnam: One to three months to test

digitalNomadVisas.hiddenH: The hidden friction after the visa
digitalNomadVisas.hiddenP1: The visa gets you into the country. It doesn't solve daily life.
digitalNomadVisas.hiddenP2: After you arrive, the smaller frictions start to matter: how you pay rent, whether your card works at small merchants, how much cash you carry, whether local apps accept your foreign card, where you take video calls, and what happens when everyone else pays through a local system you can't access.
digitalNomadVisas.hiddenP3: This is why the best digital nomad base isn't only the one with the best visa. It's the one where the small systems around your life are easiest to understand.
digitalNomadVisas.nextH: What to do next before choosing your base
nextList: Check the official visa page for the country you're considering. Don't rely only on old blog posts or social media comments.
Confirm whether the visa is for tourism, remote work, or formal residence. Those aren't the same thing.
Check the documentation early: passport validity, bank statements, income proof, employment letter, itinerary, insurance, and application timing.
Decide your real stay length. A one-month workation and a one-year base need different visa logic.
Budget for the first two weeks, not only monthly rent. Deposits, SIM cards, transport, coworking trials, ATM fees, and setup costs add up.
Refresh exchange rates before publishing or booking. Visa fees and income requirements can look very different in EUR depending on timing.
digitalNomadVisas.finalP1: For 2026, Thailand is the clearest choice if your priority is a purpose-built digital nomad route.
digitalNomadVisas.finalP2: Vietnam is the strongest option if you want a flexible, affordable, lower-commitment base for a shorter stay.
digitalNomadVisas.finalP3: Bali, Indonesia, is the best fit if you want lifestyle and community, and you have the income and employment documents for the remote worker route.
digitalNomadVisas.finalP4: The smarter question isn't "Which visa is best?" It's "Which country matches the way I actually work, spend, move, and live?"
digitalNomadVisas.finalP5: Start there. Then choose the visa.

sources.label: Royal Thai Consulate-General, Frankfurt — Destination Thailand Visa (DTV) Workation: 5-year multiple-entry validity, 180 days per entry, EUR 350 fee, financial evidence of at least 500,000 THB, remote-work or portfolio documentation.
Vietnam Immigration Department — National Electronic Visa (e-visa) portal: e-visa valid for a maximum of 90 days, single or multiple entry; fee USD 25 (single) / USD 50 (multiple).

Directorate General of Immigration, Republic of Indonesia — E33G Remote Worker Visa (evisa.imigrasi.go.id): 1-year stay, no sponsor required, fee totalling IDR 7,000,000, income of at least USD 60,000/year, employment agreement with a company outside Indonesia.

seo.title: Testing Lumi in Hanoi — A Founder Note by Gaurav Bansal
seo.description: Lumi co-founder Gaurav Bansal shares what testing the product firsthand in Hanoi taught him about real users, payment friction, and founder conviction.

hanoiFounderNote.title: I Came to Hanoi to Test Our Product. I Left More Convicted Than Ever.
hanoiFounderNote.subtitle: After months of building Lumi behind the scenes, co-founder Gaurav Bansal travelled to Hanoi to experience the product firsthand — and found the strongest lessons outside the roadmap.
hanoiFounderNote.author: Gaurav Bansal
hanoiFounderNote.imgAlt: Lumi co-founder Gaurav Bansal with travellers he met at a cafe in Hanoi, Vietnam.
paragraphs: I've always had a special connection with Hanoi.

I first visited the city almost a decade ago, and ever since then I've loved the energy here — the movement, the pace, the coffee culture, and the feeling that everything somehow works despite the chaos.
This trip, however, felt different.
I wasn't arriving as a tourist. I came here with a different purpose: to test something our team had spent months building.
At Lumi, we've been working on a payment experience designed to make spending abroad feel simple for travellers. For the end user, the product should feel seamless.
But as builders, we know simplicity is rarely simple.

Behind that experience sits months of product development, regulatory work, payment partnerships, compliance requirements, and countless iterations that users will hopefully never have to think about.
So before flying to Hanoi, I made myself one small challenge.
I would spend the trip without carrying cash.
No ATM withdrawals. No backup wallet. I wanted to experience the city exactly the way locals increasingly do today: through QR payments.
The experiment started immediately.
When I arrived at my hotel, I was given two payment options: pay in cash, or use my international card with an additional 5% fee attached.
I paid with QR instead.
No additional charge.
It sounds like a small moment, but standing there — using something we'd spent months building — felt different.
There's a quiet satisfaction in watching an idea move from internal planning to something that works in the real world.
As I moved around Hanoi over the following days, one thing became impossible to ignore.
QR payments are deeply embedded in everyday life here. Vietnam has clearly embraced digital payments at scale.
But for many travellers, access remains the challenge.
One afternoon I noticed a long ATM queue filled almost entirely with foreign visitors waiting to withdraw cash.
It genuinely surprised me.
In a country moving so quickly toward digital payments, travellers were still being pushed back into old payment habits simply because better alternatives were unavailable.
One moment especially stayed with me.
I watched a family at a cafe struggle because their card payment repeatedly failed. Eventually one family member had to leave, find an ATM, withdraw cash, and come back while everyone else waited.
It was a simple situation, but a strong reminder that payment friction still quietly shapes the travel experience far more than people realise.
The most memorable part of the trip happened unexpectedly.
I met three travellers from Spain sitting at another cafe nearby, and I casually started telling them about what we'd been building.
I expected a quick exchange and maybe a few polite questions.
Instead, one of them, Cuesto, immediately connected with the problem.

The conversation continued for almost two hours. We discussed travel experiences, payment frustrations, and the everyday challenges visitors face when navigating countries where local payment systems increasingly dominate.
What stood out to me wasn't just the conversation itself. It was watching someone outside our team immediately understand why this product should exist.
He downloaded the app. Completed the setup in just a few minutes. And became our first customer.
That moment made me quietly proud.
This trip reinforced something I believe every founder should experience early.
Product ideas are important. Strategy discussions are necessary. But there's no substitute for stepping directly into the market you're building for.
Talking to real users teaches you more than weeks of internal conversations. It gives clarity. It builds conviction. And sometimes, it reminds you why you started building in the first place.
I left Hanoi feeling more certain than ever. We're solving a very real problem.
And sometimes the best validation doesn't come from a pitch deck or roadmap. It comes from simply watching someone use what you built for the very first time.

seo.title: Why We Chose Da Nang — Lumi's Southeast Asia Launch
seo.description: Lumi, a French fintech building a euro wallet for European travellers in Southeast Asia, has chosen Da Nang as its launch community — and is inviting remote workers to shape the product.

daNangPressRelease.title: Why We Chose Da Nang
daNangPressRelease.subtitle: We're building a euro wallet for European travelers across Southeast Asia — and we've picked Da Nang as the place to launch it. Here's why, and how you can help shape what we build.
daNangPressRelease.imgAlt: The Dragon Bridge lit up at dusk over the Han River in Da Nang, Vietnam.
daNangPressRelease.leadP: Lumi, a French fintech building a euro wallet for European travelers across Southeast Asia, has chosen Da Nang as the launch community for its regional rollout. We unveiled the move at a Founding Ambassadors workshop in the city on 10 July, inviting Da Nang's international remote workers to become our first ambassadors and testers.
daNangPressRelease.leadP2: The timing isn't an accident. Our announcement lands as Da Nang hosts its Business, Finance and Technology Week (7–12 July 2026), a citywide gathering of policymakers, investors and fintech leaders headlined by the inaugural Vietnam Finance Forum on 9 and 10 July. The week is a reminder of how quickly Da Nang is becoming Vietnam's emerging center for innovation and international finance.
daNangPressRelease.problemH: The problem every visitor runs into
daNangPressRelease.problemP1: If you've spent any time in Vietnam, you already know the friction. Locals pay for almost everything — a café, a bowl of phở, a taxi — by scanning a VietQR code straight from their banking app. Foreigners can't: those QR codes require a Vietnamese bank account.
daNangPressRelease.problemP2: Lumi closes that gap. You top up a wallet in euros and pay any local QR code exactly as a resident would — one scan, in seconds, with no local bank account and no scramble for cash. Built by our engineering team in India, the app is live and already used daily by the Lumi team across Vietnam.
daNangPressRelease.whyP1: The pull of Da Nang runs deeper than the calendar. In January 2026, Vietnam inaugurated the Da Nang International Financial Center, designating the city as the country's innovation-focused financial hub, with an explicit mandate around digital payments, fintech and a regulatory sandbox for new financial models.
daNangPressRelease.whyP2: At the same time, Da Nang has become one of Southeast Asia's most popular bases for digital nomads and international remote workers — drawn by its beaches, low cost of living, fast connectivity and an unusually active scene of meetups and coworking spaces. For us, the combination is rare: a city whose public ambition and whose everyday residents both point toward precisely the kind of product we're building.
daNangPressRelease.whyP3: That direction is set at the highest level of policy. Vietnam's Resolution 57-NQ/TW, adopted by the Politburo in December 2024, places science, technology, innovation and digital transformation — including the build-out of a cashless, digital economy — at the center of national development. By bringing international visitors into Vietnam's own QR-payment ecosystem, Lumi contributes to that agenda, connecting the country's digital-transformation drive with one of its most important sectors: tourism.
daNangPressRelease.quote1: We didn't choose Da Nang by accident. It's the rare place where the people we build for — international remote workers who live between currencies — and the ambition of the city are all pulling in the same direction. Vietnam has just made Da Nang its home for digital-payments innovation, and that's exactly where a wallet like ours belongs.
daNangPressRelease.quote1By: Pierre Lahbabi, co-founder and CEO of Lumi
daNangPressRelease.ambassadorsH: Build it with us: the Founding Ambassadors program
daNangPressRelease.ambassadorsP1: Through our Founding Ambassadors program, we're inviting Da Nang's remote-work community to shape the product ahead of its wider launch. At the 10 July workshop — held from 2:00 to 4:00 p.m. at The Workshop on Chế Lan Viên in the Ngũ Hành Sơn district — participants set up the wallet, made real payments on the spot and gave direct feedback to the founding team, with free wallet credit to spend during the session. Their input will guide the app's usability and feature roadmap.
daNangPressRelease.ambassadorsP2: Beyond the workshop itself, we're enlisting European remote workers and social-media creators as ambassadors in a broader campaign that spotlights Da Nang's dynamism as a center of innovation — and the wallet's rollout with local partners such as hotels, restaurants and everyday merchants across the city.
daNangPressRelease.quote2: Paying a street-food stall or a neighborhood café should feel the same for a visitor as it does for a local: one scan, and it's done. That everyday moment is what we're perfecting here, alongside the people who will use it most.
daNangPressRelease.nextP1: Lumi plans to bring the same local-QR experience to its other priority markets in the region — Thailand (PromptPay) and Indonesia (QRIS) — as it scales toward a full regional launch.
daNangPressRelease.quote3: Cross-border payments in Southeast Asia is a large, underserved market, and Lumi is tackling it from the right end — the everyday friction every traveler feels. Basing the launch in Da Nang, just as the city steps up as a hub for digital-payments innovation, is a sharp and deliberate move, and exactly the kind of team and timing worth getting behind.
daNangPressRelease.quote3By: Robert Brice Cerival, Senior Advisor to Lumi in Vietnam
daNangPressRelease.aboutP: Lumi is a French fintech building a euro wallet that lets European travelers pay by local QR code across Southeast Asia (VietQR in Vietnam, PromptPay in Thailand and QRIS in Indonesia) as easily as residents do. Founded near Paris, Lumi was co-founded by CEO Pierre Lahbabi, a graduate of France's École Polytechnique and Mines Paris, and a payments specialist with a career spanning banking and technology consulting. Co-founder and COO Gaurav Bansal brings more than fifteen years in fintech product and technology consulting, with roles at Sopra Steria, Capgemini and fintech lender Biz2Credit, and holds a master's in finance from India's National Institute of Securities Markets. Learn more at lumifin.io.

seo.title: Cross-Border QR Payments Are Growing — But Who Can Access Them?
seo.description: Southeast Asia recorded 36.2 million cross-border QR transactions in 2025. Yet European travellers still often cannot pay by local QR code. Why access, not adoption, is the real challenge.

crossBorderQrAccess.title: Cross-Border QR Payments Are Growing. The Next Challenge Is Who Can Access Them
crossBorderQrAccess.subtitle: Southeast Asia's QR networks are becoming more connected. But for European travellers, the ability to pay still often depends on having the right local or regional bank account.
crossBorderQrAccess.author: Tanvi Nag
crossBorderQrAccess.imgAlt: A European traveller scanning a VietQR code at the counter of an independent café in Vietnam, with the merchant visible in the background.
crossBorderQrAccess.imgCaption: Local QR payments are becoming more connected across Southeast Asia, but access still depends on the user's bank and payment provider.
crossBorderQrAccess.introP1: At a café in Ho Chi Minh City, paying can take seconds. A customer opens a banking app, scans the merchant's VietQR code and confirms the amount. No card terminal changes hands. No cash needs to be counted.
crossBorderQrAccess.introP2: For a local customer, the experience feels almost invisible.
crossBorderQrAccess.introP3: For a European traveller standing beside them, that same QR code may be unusable.
crossBorderQrAccess.introP4: This is the tension at the centre of Southeast Asia's payment transformation. The region has built fast, familiar and increasingly connected QR-payment networks. Cross-border usage is growing quickly. Yet access still depends heavily on where someone banks, which app they use and whether their financial institution participates in a particular payment linkage.
crossBorderQrAccess.introP5: The next challenge is no longer simply making QR payments work across borders. It is making them accessible to more of the people crossing those borders.
crossBorderQrAccess.behaviourH: Cross-border QR payments are becoming real behaviour
crossBorderQrAccess.behaviourP1: In April 2026, ASEAN finance ministers and central bank governors reported that the region had established 29 QR and person-to-person instant-payment linkages within ASEAN and with external partners by the end of 2025.
crossBorderQrAccess.behaviourP2: Usage is no longer limited to small technical pilots. During 2025, cross-border QR payments reached:
crossBorderQrAccess.behaviourP3: These figures show clear momentum. Travellers, households and businesses are beginning to use regional payment connections in everyday situations, not only in controlled demonstrations.
crossBorderQrAccess.behaviourP4: The direction makes sense. Domestic QR schemes already have strong local acceptance. VietQR in Vietnam, PromptPay in Thailand and QRIS in Indonesia allow consumers to pay everyone from established retailers to small independent merchants. Connecting these networks across borders can extend an experience people already understand instead of asking merchants to adopt another payment method.
crossBorderQrAccess.behaviourP5: That is a powerful starting point.
crossBorderQrAccess.howH: How regional QR payment links work
crossBorderQrAccess.howP1: A cross-border QR linkage allows a customer from one participating country to scan a merchant QR code in another participating country using a supported banking or payment app.
crossBorderQrAccess.howP2: Behind the simple scan, several things need to happen:
howList: The customer's app reads the merchant's local QR code.
The payment request moves between participating payment systems or providers.
The amount is converted between currencies.
Compliance, fraud and transaction checks take place.
The merchant receives funds through the local payment network.
crossBorderQrAccess.howP3: The customer sees one transaction. Underneath it sits a coordinated network of banks, payment operators, foreign-exchange providers and regulatory frameworks.
crossBorderQrAccess.howP4: This model can work very well for customers whose banks are already connected. A traveller from Thailand may be able to scan a supported QR code in a neighbouring market with their Thai banking app, for example.
crossBorderQrAccess.howP5: But connectivity between countries does not automatically create universal access.
crossBorderQrAccess.gapP1: Imagine arriving in Vietnam with a French bank account, a euro balance and a widely used European finance app.
crossBorderQrAccess.gapP2: You may have sufficient funds. Your identity may already have been verified by a regulated European institution. Your phone may be capable of scanning the code. Yet your banking app still cannot initiate a payment through VietQR.
crossBorderQrAccess.gapP3: Why? Because the issue is not the QR image itself. The issue is access to the payment network behind it.
crossBorderQrAccess.gapP4: Most cross-border QR arrangements connect selected domestic or regional institutions. They do not automatically connect every foreign bank account or wallet. This leaves many European travellers relying on a familiar set of alternatives:

optionsRows.friction: ATM fees, carrying cash and repeated withdrawals
Foreign-exchange costs, possible surcharges and limited acceptance among smaller merchants
Often unavailable or impractical for short-term visitors
Usually requires an account with a supported institution

crossBorderQrAccess.gapP5: None of these options is universally bad. Cards remain useful, and cash is still essential in many situations. The problem appears when a traveller has money but cannot use the payment method sitting directly in front of them.
crossBorderQrAccess.gapP6: That is an access problem, not an adoption problem.
crossBorderQrAccess.localH: Local networks are already winning at checkout
crossBorderQrAccess.localP1: Much of the global payments conversation focuses on creating new ways to pay. Southeast Asia offers a different lesson: the most effective customer interface may already exist.
crossBorderQrAccess.localP2: Merchants understand the QR code on their counter. Customers understand the scanning motion. Domestic payment networks already handle local acceptance and settlement. Replacing that system would create unnecessary work for both sides.
crossBorderQrAccess.localQuestion: How can a traveller fund a payment from abroad while allowing the merchant to receive money through the local network they already use?
crossBorderQrAccess.localP4: Answering that question requires connections between different forms of money, institutions and regulatory environments. It also requires a customer experience that hides most of that complexity.
crossBorderQrAccess.stablecoinH: Where stablecoins may fit, and where they do not
crossBorderQrAccess.stablecoinP1: Stablecoins are often presented as an instant solution to cross-border payments. The current evidence calls for a more measured view.
crossBorderQrAccess.stablecoinP2: In July 2026, the Financial Stability Board noted that stablecoins represented, by some estimates, less than 0.2% of total cross-border payment volume in 2025. Their role remains small compared with the wider market.
crossBorderQrAccess.stablecoinP3: The FSB also pointed toward a potentially more realistic near-term use: stablecoins as components in hybrid models, integrated with bank money, foreign exchange and established settlement systems.
crossBorderQrAccess.stablecoinP5: For a traveller, the goal is not necessarily to buy, hold or manage a digital asset. The goal is to fund a payment in a familiar currency and pay a merchant through the appropriate local network.
crossBorderQrAccess.stablecoinP6: Stablecoins may help providers move value between parts of that journey more efficiently. But they are only one part of the infrastructure. They do not remove the need for:
crossBorderQrAccess.stablecoinP7: The most useful stablecoin payment may therefore be one the customer never has to see.
crossBorderQrAccess.guardrailH: The guardrails are part of the product
crossBorderQrAccess.guardrailP1: Payment infrastructure is not valuable only because it moves quickly. It must also move money safely, predictably and within the rules of each market.
crossBorderQrAccess.guardrailP2: ASEAN's own 2026 statement highlights the need to manage fraud risks, align oversight practices and improve resilience as payment connectivity expands. This is particularly important as scams increasingly move across platforms and borders.
crossBorderQrAccess.guardrailP3: For providers connecting European funding sources with Southeast Asian payment networks, compliance cannot be added after the customer experience is designed. It shapes the experience from the beginning.
guardrailList: who is eligible to use the service;
which regulated partners handle each part of the flow;
what information customers receive about fees and exchange rates;
how failed or disputed payments are resolved.
crossBorderQrAccess.guardrailP5: Guardrails can feel invisible when they work properly. But they are what turn technical connectivity into dependable payment infrastructure.
crossBorderQrAccess.nextPhaseH: What this means for the next phase of QR payments
crossBorderQrAccess.nextPhaseP1: The growth of cross-border QR transactions proves that regional interoperability can translate into real usage. The next phase will require the industry to widen access without weakening trust.
crossBorderQrAccess.nextPhaseP2: For European travellers, that could mean being able to:
nextPhaseList: fund from a familiar European account;
complete verification once in a secure flow;
scan the local QR code already accepted by the merchant;
see the amount and exchange rate clearly;
pay without opening a local bank account;
leave the underlying settlement process to regulated providers.
crossBorderQrAccess.nextPhaseP3: This is the experience Lumifin is building, beginning in Vietnam. Users fund in euros and pay local merchants through VietQR, while the cross-border infrastructure and compliance processes remain behind the scenes.
crossBorderQrAccess.nextPhaseP4: The aim is not to replace the payment system that already works locally. It is to build a safe bridge into it.
crossBorderQrAccess.beforeTripH: Before your next trip to Southeast Asia
crossBorderQrAccess.beforeTripP1: QR-payment access still varies by country, bank and provider. Before travelling:
beforeTripList: check whether your banking or payment app supports QR payments in your destination;
carry a backup card and a modest amount of cash;
review foreign transaction and ATM fees;
never scan a QR code that appears altered or placed over another code;
confirm the merchant name and payment amount before approving;
download payment or travel apps only from official sources;
complete any required identity checks before you need to make a payment.
crossBorderQrAccess.beforeTripP2: Southeast Asia's payment networks are becoming more connected with each year. The opportunity now is to ensure that the people arriving from outside those networks can participate safely too.

seo.title: Scooter, Grab or Metro? Getting Around Vietnam
seo.description: Compare scooters, Grab, taxis, buses and metro travel in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang, with practical safety, licence and payment advice.

gettingAroundVietnam.title: Scooter, Grab or Metro? Getting Around Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang
gettingAroundVietnam.subtitle: Scooters are everywhere in Vietnam. That does not mean your holiday should double as your first riding lesson. Here is how to choose the safest, smartest way around each city.
gettingAroundVietnam.author: Pierre Lahbabi
gettingAroundVietnam.imgAlt: A European traveller standing on the pavement in Vietnam, checking a transport app while scooters pass on the street.
gettingAroundVietnam.kerbH: The scooter question starts at the kerb
gettingAroundVietnam.kerbP1: Step outside in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City or Da Nang and the first thing you notice is movement. Scooters stream around buses, collect outside cafés and fill every gap at a red light. From the pavement, riding one can look like the most natural way to join the city.
gettingAroundVietnam.kerbP2: It is also easy to confuse familiarity with simplicity. Vietnamese riders grow up reading traffic patterns that can feel unpredictable to a visitor. The World Health Organization says motorcycles make up more than 90% of vehicles in Vietnam and are involved in over 60% of road crashes.
gettingAroundVietnam.shortAnswerP: If you cannot already ride confidently, Vietnam is not the place to learn. If you are experienced, correctly licensed and insured, a scooter may make sense in selected places — most plausibly Da Nang, and least plausibly central Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City.

optionsRows.payment: In app, card where supported, or cash
Usually cash or local ticket system

gettingAroundVietnam.optionsNote: *Indicative planning ranges only. App prices vary by distance, demand, weather and time; verify the live fare before booking.
gettingAroundVietnam.hanoiP1: Hanoi rewards slow exploration. The Old Quarter is dense, crossings demand attention and many short journeys are easier on foot than they first appear. For longer trips, GrabBike is efficient if you are comfortable riding as a passenger; GrabCar or a reputable taxi is calmer with luggage, rain or more than one person.
gettingAroundVietnam.hanoiP2: The city's metro lines can be useful when your route matches them, while buses offer broader coverage at low cost. Neither replaces every journey, so most visitors will mix walking, ride-hailing and public transport.
gettingAroundVietnam.hanoiVerdict: City verdict: Do not learn to ride here. Even experienced visitors may find that parking, navigation and traffic awareness erase the supposed convenience of a rental scooter.
gettingAroundVietnam.hcmcH: Ho Chi Minh City: ride-hailing wins on flexibility
gettingAroundVietnam.hcmcP1: Ho Chi Minh City is large, fast and spread across districts. GrabBike is often the quickest way through traffic for one person travelling light. GrabCar is more comfortable in heavy rain, with bags, or after dark. The city's first metro line gives travellers a useful alternative along its corridor, but it does not yet cover every neighbourhood you are likely to visit.
gettingAroundVietnam.hcmcP2: A rental scooter can look efficient on a map. In practice, lane changes, buses, delivery riders, unfamiliar junctions and sudden tropical rain create a steep learning curve. The cost saving is rarely worth the risk for a beginner.
gettingAroundVietnam.hcmcVerdict: City verdict: Use GrabBike, GrabCar, taxis and the metro. Self-riding should be reserved for confident, legally licensed and properly insured riders — not first-timers.
gettingAroundVietnam.daNangH: Da Nang: the strongest case for experienced riders
gettingAroundVietnam.daNangP1: Da Nang is more open, less dense and easier to navigate than Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City. Beaches and attractions are spread along wide roads, which makes a scooter genuinely useful for some travellers. It is still traffic, not a training ground.
gettingAroundVietnam.daNangP2: If you already ride confidently, have the correct licence documentation, confirm that your insurance covers the vehicle and route, and rent a roadworthy scooter with a proper helmet, Da Nang is the most reasonable of the three cities for self-riding. Grab remains widely practical when you want none of that admin — or when rain arrives.
gettingAroundVietnam.daNangVerdict: City verdict: Best of the three for experienced riders. Beginners should still choose Grab or a car with a driver.
gettingAroundVietnam.rentalH: Before renting a scooter: the checks people skip
gettingAroundVietnam.rentalP1: A rental shop handing you the keys does not prove you are legally entitled or insured to ride. Rules can depend on your licence category, nationality, international permit and engine size. Insurance policies may exclude riding without the exact documents required locally.
rentalChecks: Check the latest Vietnamese requirements and your home-country travel advice before departure.
Confirm that your licence category covers the scooter's engine size and that any required international driving permit is valid in Vietnam.
Ask your insurer in writing whether motorcycle or scooter riding is covered, including medical care, third-party liability and repatriation.
Photograph the scooter before departure; test the brakes, lights, indicators, tyres and horn.
Use a properly fitting helmet. Do not ride after drinking, during heavy rain or when tired.
Never leave your passport as informal collateral if a safer deposit arrangement is available.
gettingAroundVietnam.rentalDisclaimer: This is general travel information, not legal or insurance advice. Requirements change, so verify them with official authorities and your insurer before riding.
gettingAroundVietnam.trippedH: Where European travellers get tripped up
gettingAroundVietnam.trippedCardH: The app accepts your card — until it does not
gettingAroundVietnam.trippedCardP: Ride-hailing apps may accept an international card during setup, then decline it later because of issuer controls, authentication or fraud checks. Keep a second payment method and some small-denomination cash.
gettingAroundVietnam.trippedCashP: Some bookings are configured as cash rides, and independent taxis or buses may not accept foreign cards. Check the selected payment method before confirming, rather than discovering it at the kerb.
gettingAroundVietnam.trippedCheapH: The cheapest ride is not always the easiest ride
gettingAroundVietnam.trippedCheapP: A low fare can hide practical friction: finding the pickup point, carrying luggage on a motorbike, waiting through a storm or explaining a destination. Choose for the journey you are actually making, not just the smallest number on screen.
gettingAroundVietnam.setupH: The smartest setup for each city
setupList: Hanoi: Walk within neighbourhoods; use GrabBike for confident passengers, GrabCar or taxis for comfort, and metro or buses when the route fits.
Ho Chi Minh City: Use GrabBike for fast solo trips, GrabCar in rain or with luggage, and the metro along its operating corridor.
Da Nang: Use Grab by default. Consider a rental scooter only if you are already experienced, correctly licensed and insured.
appsList: Google Maps — walking, driving and some public-transport planning.
A translation app with Vietnamese downloaded offline.
Your bank app — to approve authentication and monitor transactions.
Lumifin — for eligible travellers who want to fund in euros and pay through local QR rails where supported.
checklist: Install and verify your ride-hailing account before you need an airport pickup.
Add a primary and backup payment method.
Carry small notes for cash-only rides and buses.
Confirm the vehicle plate and driver inside the app before getting in or on.
Use the helmet provided for motorbike rides and ask for another if it does not fit.
Check rain and air-quality conditions before choosing an open-air ride.
Save your accommodation address in Vietnamese.
If you are considering a rental, pause and verify licence and insurance first.
gettingAroundVietnam.bottomP1: Vietnam does not require every visitor to become a scooter rider. Hanoi is often best understood neighbourhood by neighbourhood. Ho Chi Minh City rewards a mix of ride-hailing and metro. Da Nang offers the clearest case for a scooter — but only for people who already know how to ride and have the paperwork and insurance to match.
gettingAroundVietnam.bottomP2: The goal is not to move exactly like a local on day one. It is to choose the option that lets you experience the city without turning the journey itself into the biggest risk of the trip.

seo.title: MoMo, ZaloPay, VNPay: Vietnam's E-Wallets Decoded
seo.description: MoMo, ZaloPay and VNPay run most of Vietnam's QR payments, but they were built around a Vietnamese ID. What each one is, and what actually works for a European visitor.

vietnameseEWallets.title: MoMo, ZaloPay, VNPay: The Vietnamese E-Wallet Landscape Decoded
vietnameseEWallets.subtitle: Three names sit behind most of Vietnam's QR payments. They are not interchangeable — and the differences matter more for a visitor than for the locals who use them daily.
vietnameseEWallets.author: Gaurav Bansal
vietnameseEWallets.imgAlt: A printed QR sticker propped against a coffee cart near Ben Thanh Market, with a customer's phone mid-scan.
vietnameseEWallets.introP1: You order a cà phê sữa đá at a cart near Ben Thanh Market. It's 30,000 VND (about €1). You reach for coins, and the vendor slides a laminated square across the counter — a QR code (Quick Response code, the pixelated black-and-white pattern you scan with a phone). She's not expecting your cash. She's expecting you to scan.
vietnameseEWallets.introP2: For a first-time European visitor, that small square is where Vietnam stops feeling familiar. At home you tap a card. Here, a barefoot noodle stall, a Grab driver, and a rooftop bar in District 1 all want the same thing: a scan. And the three names behind most of those scans are MoMo, ZaloPay, and VNPay.
vietnameseEWallets.introP3: They are not interchangeable, and the differences matter more for you — a visitor — than for the locals who use them daily. Here's what each one actually is, and which parts of this system you can realistically plug into on a two-week trip.
vietnameseEWallets.whyThreeH: Why there are three names, not one
vietnameseEWallets.whyThreeP1: Vietnam went cashless fast. In 2025, the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV — the country's central bank) reported that the total value of cashless payments reached nearly 28 times the country's GDP, with QR code transactions surging by more than 100% in volume in a single year. There are now over 232 million individual payment accounts in a country of around 100 million people. Meanwhile ATM transactions are shrinking, and POS (point-of-sale) terminals grew almost 20% in a year.
vietnameseEWallets.whyThreeP2: That growth didn't produce one winner. It produced a layered system: consumer wallets you download, a messaging app that quietly became a wallet, and the payment "rails" running underneath both. MoMo, ZaloPay, and VNPay sit in different layers, which is exactly why locals happily use all three and rarely think about it.
vietnameseEWallets.momoH: MoMo: the super app everyone means
vietnameseEWallets.momoP1: When a Vietnamese friend says "just MoMo me," they mean the wallet roughly two-thirds of e-wallet users in the country have on their phone — around 30 million people, by industry surveys. MoMo is the closest thing Vietnam has to a super app: one place to pay a merchant, split a dinner bill, top up mobile data, buy cinema tickets, pay an electricity bill, and send money to a friend.
vietnameseEWallets.momoP2: For a local, MoMo is the default for peer-to-peer (P2P — person-to-person) transfers and everyday spending. You'll see its pink logo on stickers at street stalls from Hanoi's Old Quarter to Da Nang's beachfront cafés. If Vietnam had one wallet you'd want in your pocket, this is the one people would name.
vietnameseEWallets.momoP3: The catch, which we'll come back to, is that MoMo was built around the Vietnamese national ID. That makes it powerful for residents and awkward for tourists.
vietnameseEWallets.zaloH: ZaloPay: the wallet hiding inside your chat app
vietnameseEWallets.zaloP1: ZaloPay is the payment arm of Zalo — Vietnam's dominant messaging app, the WhatsApp of the country. Almost everyone here already has Zalo open all day, so ZaloPay rides along inside an app people never close.
vietnameseEWallets.zaloP2: That gives it a different feel from MoMo. Sending money can happen right inside a chat, the way you'd send a message. ZaloPay has also pushed harder on breadth of payment methods — bank transfers, international cards, Apple Pay — and on higher-end financial products like savings features. Industry data puts it a clear second among wallets by usage.
vietnameseEWallets.zaloP3: For visitors, ZaloPay has one quietly useful trait: of the big wallets, it's the one most often reported to accept passport-based sign-up rather than demanding a national ID. "Most often" is not "reliably" — but if you're going to try a local wallet, this is a sensible first attempt.
vietnameseEWallets.vnpayH: VNPay: the rails you'll use without downloading anything
vietnameseEWallets.vnpayP1: VNPay is the one most travellers use without ever installing it. Rather than a consumer wallet you scroll through, it's largely payment infrastructure — the VNPAY-QR network that banks plug their own apps into, with more than 350,000 acceptance points nationwide. When a local opens their Vietcombank or Techcombank app to scan a merchant's code, there's a good chance VNPay's rails are running underneath. There's also a standalone VNPAY app aimed at travellers, which we'll come back to.
vietnameseEWallets.vnpayP2: But VNPay is really one player riding something bigger — the shared standard that lets all these apps read the very same code, and that standard is the part actually worth understanding.
vietnameseEWallets.vietqrH: VietQR: the standard that quietly makes all of this work
vietnameseEWallets.vietqrP1: VietQR is Vietnam's national QR standard, run by NAPAS — the National Payment Corporation of Vietnam, the central switch that clears transfers between the country's banks in real time, around the clock, in under ten seconds. Think of NAPAS as the roundabout every bank's traffic passes through, and VietQR as the single road sign everyone agrees to read.
vietnameseEWallets.vietqrP2: Before VietQR, a merchant might tape up a MoMo code, a ZaloPay code and a separate bank code side by side, and you had to match the app to the sticker. Since the standard launched in 2021 — built by NAPAS with Agribank, BIDV, VietinBank and Vietcombank, and aligned to both the SBV's rules and the global EMVCo QR spec (the same base standard behind QR payments worldwide) — that mess is gone. One printed square now accepts a scan from almost any participating Vietnamese bank app or wallet, and the money settles bank-account to bank-account behind the scenes. It caught on fast: VietQR transactions were still growing more than 100% a year into 2024, and roughly six in ten Vietnamese now reach for a QR code routinely.
vietnameseEWallets.vietqrP3: The word that matters is interoperable. Because VietQR is an open, shared standard rather than one company's private network, the code on the counter doesn't care which app reads it — it only cares that the app speaks VietQR. NAPAS has even begun extending that reach across borders, letting visitors from Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and China pay through their home apps. That one design choice — open, not walled — is what makes the next part possible.

vietnameseEWallets.frictionH: The part nobody tells European visitors
vietnameseEWallets.frictionP1: Here's the friction. Since 2025, Vietnam has tightened identity rules on e-wallets, and biometric and ID verification is now standard for wallet users. That was designed to cut fraud — and it works well for residents with a Vietnamese national ID and a local bank account. For a European here for twelve days, it's a wall.
vietnameseEWallets.frictionP2: In practice, three things trip people up. First, most wallet sign-ups expect a Vietnamese phone number, which means buying a local SIM (easy and cheap — a tourist SIM runs roughly 100,000–200,000 VND, about €3.50–€6.50 — at any airport kiosk). Second, the smoothest setup still runs through a local bank account, which generally requires a temporary residence card or a longer-stay visa you won't have on a tourist entry. Third, verification acceptance is inconsistent: a passport works on one app version and not the next.
vietnameseEWallets.frictionP3: One habit worth adopting from locals, regardless of which app you use: after you scan a code, check the recipient name that pops up before you confirm. Fake QR stickers pasted over real ones are the most common scam, and that one glance defeats most of them.
vietnameseEWallets.worksH: What actually works if you're here for two weeks
vietnameseEWallets.worksP1: Don't fight the resident system. Reach for the parts built for someone in your position — a visitor, not a resident.
vietnameseEWallets.worksP2: The friction all traces back to one thing: MoMo, ZaloPay and VNPay were built around a Vietnamese ID and a Vietnamese bank account. VietQR wasn't. Because the standard is open, it will accept a scan from any app that speaks it — and that's the doorway a European wallet can walk through. It's the gap Lumifin is closing: you top it up in euros from your European account, and it pays those same VietQR codes directly — the very network behind that coffee-cart sticker — so there's no local SIM, no local bank account and no biometric hoop to clear. The euro-to-dong rate shows before you confirm, and it charges one flat fee (2%) rather than the layered card surcharges and airport-counter markups that quietly cost more. It's live in Vietnam right now and rolling out gradually, which is worth knowing before you lean on it as your only method.
vietnameseEWallets.worksP3: Whatever wallet you carry, keep two companions. Grab — the ride-and-food app you'll use anyway — has its own built-in wallet (Moca) and takes international cards, so rides and a lot of food are covered on their own. And keep a modest cash buffer: a bánh mì is around 25,000 VND (€0.85), a bowl of phở about 60,000 VND (€2), and the smallest carts still take notes gratefully when a scan won't go through. (If you'd rather ride the local rails directly, the VNPAY traveller app also lets you register with a passport and an international card.)
vietnameseEWallets.worksP4: That combination — a euro-funded wallet that speaks VietQR, Grab, and a little cash — covers a District 1 rooftop, a beach café at An Bang near Hoi An, and the Ben Thanh coffee cart where this started.
vietnameseEWallets.calloutBody: Made for this exact trip: Lumifin pays Vietnam's VietQR codes straight from a euro balance — interbank rate shown up front, one flat fee, no local SIM or bank account.
vietnameseEWallets.nextP1: Before you fly: set up a euro-funded wallet that works on Vietnam's QR rails — Lumifin is built for exactly this — and download Grab. On arrival, top up, run one small test payment at a convenience store, and keep about 500,000 VND (roughly €17) in cash for the stalls that still prefer it. Do that in your first hour on the ground, and the QR square on the counter stops being a wall — it just becomes how you pay.

seo.title: Why Your Card Gets Declined at Vietnamese Street Vendors
seo.description: Five different failures hide behind one word on the screen. What each decline actually means in Vietnam, and which ones you can fix before your flight.

cardDeclinedVietnam.title: Why Your Visa or Mastercard Gets Declined at Vietnamese Street Vendors
cardDeclinedVietnam.subtitle: Five different failures hide behind one word on the screen. Here is what each one actually means, and which ones you can fix before your flight.
cardDeclinedVietnam.author: Gaurav Bansal
cardDeclinedVietnam.imgAlt: A card terminal showing DECLINED at a Hanoi street food stall, with a VietQR payment stand on the counter beside it.
cardDeclinedVietnam.ratesNote: Rates used in this piece: 1 EUR = 30,500 VND and 1 EUR = 38.1 THB, mid-market on 25 August 2026.
cardDeclinedVietnam.stallP1: It is 8:40 in the evening on Hàng Bạc, in Hanoi's Old Quarter. The bún chả is 60,000 đồng, about €1.97. You hold out a Visa card, because it worked in Lisbon, in Athens, and at the airport taxi rank three hours ago.
cardDeclinedVietnam.stallP2: The woman at the grill smiles, shakes her head once, and taps a laminated square of paper taped to the counter. There is no terminal. There was never a terminal. Behind you, a man in a delivery jacket scans that square, waits for a chirp from a phone speaker, and takes his food.
cardDeclinedVietnam.stallP3: Now move the scene to a café on Nguyễn Huệ in Ho Chi Minh City, where there is a terminal. You tap. The screen thinks for eleven seconds and shows DECLINED. The staff member shrugs, apologetic, and turns the QR stand around to face you instead.
cardDeclinedVietnam.stallP4: Two failures, one word, completely different causes. In payments, "declined" is doing an enormous amount of work. Let us separate the five things it can mean, because four of them have nothing to do with you having no money.
cardDeclinedVietnam.oneH: Failure one: nobody ever signed up for the system your card lives in
cardDeclinedVietnam.oneP1: This is the most common one, and it is not really a decline at all. It is an absence.
cardDeclinedVietnam.oneP2: To accept a Visa or Mastercard, a vendor needs a merchant account. That means a registered business, a bank relationship, a contract with an acquirer, a terminal that costs money every month, and settlement that lands a day or two later. A woman running a grill on a pavement has none of those things and does not want them.
cardDeclinedVietnam.oneP3: To accept VietQR, she needs a printed sheet of A4 paper. The money arrives in her personal bank account in about two seconds. Cost to her: effectively nothing.
cardDeclinedVietnam.oneP4: That gap explains almost everything. A Vietnamese café taking cards pays roughly 3 percent once issuer, network, acquirer and currency costs are added up. The same café taking VietQR often pays under 0.3 percent, and sometimes zero, because NAPAS keeps the rail cheap and banks give merchants QR for free to win them. On a 60,000 đồng bowl of noodles the difference is small. On a month of dinners it is rent. But the fee is not even the deciding factor here. The paperwork is.
cardDeclinedVietnam.oneP5: The scale of the alternative is worth sitting with. Fifteen years ago Vietnam ran on cash, with roughly 99 percent of retail in banknotes. The State Bank of Vietnam reported non-cash payments growing more than 50 percent by transaction count in 2024, with QR payments more than doubling on their own. NAPAS launched VietQR in 2021 as a shared code format every Vietnamese bank app can read, which is why a Vietcombank customer can pay a Techcombank merchant by pointing a phone at a piece of paper.
cardDeclinedVietnam.oneP6: Your card did not get rejected. It showed up to a party that moved venue.
cardDeclinedVietnam.twoH: Failure two: your own bank made a judgement call, and it guessed no
cardDeclinedVietnam.twoP1: This one surprises people, because the money is right there in the account.
cardDeclinedVietnam.twoP2: When a card issued in the European Economic Area is used at a merchant acquired outside it, the payment is what the industry calls "one leg out". Strong Customer Authentication under PSD2 binds your bank, but it does not bind the Vietnamese acquirer on the other side. The European Banking Authority addressed this directly in its Q&A on the scope of the SCA rules: where the acquirer sits outside the EEA and cannot support authentication, the issuer has to decide for itself whether to block the payment or carry the liability if it turns out to be fraud.
cardDeclinedVietnam.twoP3: Read that again, because it is the whole story. Your bank is being asked to approve a small, unfamiliar transaction, in a country you have never spent in, at a merchant it has never seen, with no authentication step available to it, and it eats the loss if it is wrong.
cardDeclinedVietnam.twoP4: So it declines. Then, once a few of your payments have gone through in Hanoi, the risk model relaxes and the same card works fine. This is why the first attempt on day one fails and the fourth attempt on day two sails through, and why nothing you did in between actually mattered.
cardDeclinedVietnam.twoP5: Fixable, mostly. Set a travel notification in your banking app before you fly. Check whether your card has a geographic block toggle switched on by default, because several European neobanks ship with one. And carry a second card issued by a different bank, not a second card from the same one, since two cards from the same issuer share the same risk engine and will refuse you in unison.
cardDeclinedVietnam.threeH: Failure three: the terminal is fine, the connection is not
cardDeclinedVietnam.threeP1: Where terminals do exist in markets and food courts, many run over mobile data or a shared hotspot, not a fixed line. At Bến Thành Market on a Saturday afternoon, several hundred people are competing for the same cell.
cardDeclinedVietnam.threeP2: When the authorisation request times out on the way to the acquirer, the terminal has nothing useful to display, so it prints a generic refusal. The most common code in the world, ISO 8583 response 05, translates as "Do Not Honour", which is the payments equivalent of a shrug. It means the issuer said no, or something in the chain said no on the issuer's behalf, and nobody is going to tell you which.
cardDeclinedVietnam.threeP3: Practical read: if the terminal spun for a long time before failing, that is a network story, not a money story. Ask to try once. If it fails again, stop trying. Repeated attempts on the same card in the same minute look exactly like card testing to a fraud model, and you may get the card frozen for your trouble.
cardDeclinedVietnam.fourH: Failure four: the machine says yes, and that is worse
cardDeclinedVietnam.fourP1: Sometimes the terminal offers you a favour. "Pay in EUR?" it asks, with a nice round number on the screen.
cardDeclinedVietnam.fourP2: This is Dynamic Currency Conversion, or DCC, where the merchant's payment provider converts the amount at its own rate instead of letting your card network do it. The markup typically runs 3 to 8 percent and goes to the provider and the merchant, not to you. A 1,200,000 đồng dinner in District 1 is €39.34 at the real rate. Accept the EUR screen at an 8 percent spread and you have paid about €42.50 for the same food.
cardDeclinedVietnam.fourP3: Always press the local currency. Đồng in Vietnam, baht in Thailand. If the staff member has already selected EUR for you, ask for the transaction to be voided and rerun. In a card-present setting you are entitled to choose, and most terminals in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City will show both options if you look for two seconds.
cardDeclinedVietnam.fiveH: Failure five: that QR code is not a card rail, and it cannot become one
cardDeclinedVietnam.fiveP1: Here is the part travellers find genuinely counterintuitive. The vendor who cannot take your Visa is running a payment system that is faster, cheaper, and more reliable than the one your card uses. You just cannot get onto it.
cardDeclinedVietnam.fiveP2: VietQR is not a card network with a QR skin. It is a domestic instant bank transfer rail. Scanning a code tells your bank to push money from your account to the vendor's account, directly, with no acquirer, no interchange, and no settlement delay. A Visa card has no way to originate that instruction, because Visa is not a Vietnamese bank.
cardDeclinedVietnam.fiveP3: To get onto the rail as an individual, you need three things, all issued in Vietnam: a chip national ID card, a Vietnamese mobile number registered against that identity, and a Vietnamese bank account. A tourist visa stamp gets you none of them. That wall is deliberate. It is how anti-money-laundering rules are enforced at the account level, and it is a large part of why fraud rates on Vietnamese wallets stay low compared with regional peers.
cardDeclinedVietnam.fiveP4: The linkages that do exist are regional, not global. Vietnamese travellers can already scan Thai PromptPay codes with their bank apps, and Thai visitors can scan VietQR here. Links with Singapore's PayNow and Cambodia's KHQR are in progress, and Project Nexus, the BIS-led effort to connect real-time systems across the region, is expected to go live during 2026.
cardDeclinedVietnam.fiveP5: Notice who is not on any of those lists. A card issued in Paris, Madrid or Berlin sits outside every one of those corridors.

diagnosisRows.cause: No merchant account, no terminal, never was one
diagnosisRows.action: Pay by QR or cash. Do not negotiate

diagnosisRows.seen: "Do Not Honour" after a fast response
diagnosisRows.cause: Your issuer's risk engine declined a one-leg-out payment
diagnosisRows.action: Try a card from a different bank, then set a travel notice

diagnosisRows.seen: Long spin, then a generic decline
diagnosisRows.cause: Authorisation timed out over mobile data
diagnosisRows.action: One retry. If it fails again, switch payment method

diagnosisRows.cause: DCC, with a 3 to 8 percent spread added
Daily foreign spend cap or an authorisation hold
diagnosisRows.action: Check limits in the app, raise the cap, retry

cardDeclinedVietnam.gapH: The gap we built Lumi to close
cardDeclinedVietnam.gapP1: Everything above describes one structural fact: Vietnam built an excellent payment system and closed the door to visitors, not out of hostility, but because identity rules are the price of low fraud.
cardDeclinedVietnam.gapP2: Lumi is our answer to that. It is a euro wallet for EU and EEA residents, funded by SEPA transfer from your own bank account, that pays Vietnamese QR codes directly. You scan the same laminated VietQR sheet the person ahead of you in the queue just scanned, confirm with a PIN or your face, and the vendor gets đồng in their account in seconds. No Vietnamese ID, no local bank account, no borrowed MoMo from a friend. One flat 2 percent fee, with the exchange rate shown before you confirm, and payments from €1 upward so a 25,000 đồng iced coffee is a normal thing to pay for.
cardDeclinedVietnam.gapP3: Lumi is live in Vietnam right now, with Thailand and Indonesia next. Our users in Đà Nẵng and Hội An have been paying for boat rides, café bills and market food with it for months.
cardDeclinedVietnam.gapP4: None of this makes cards useless. Keep one for hotels, flights and Grab, which take foreign cards without complaint. Keep some cash for the last stall on the street that still prefers it. The point is not to replace your wallet. It is to stop the daily friction where your card and the vendor's rail have no way to meet.
cardDeclinedVietnam.ctaBody: Pay like the person in front of you. Download Lumi, finish onboarding and say hi on WhatsApp for a €5 coupon code toward your first trip.
cardDeclinedVietnam.nextP1: Before you fly, five minutes of setup saves a week of friction:
nextList: Set a travel notification in your banking app, and check for a "block payments abroad" toggle that may be on by default.
Pack two cards issued by two different banks. Same-issuer pairs fail together.
Note your daily foreign transaction limit and raise it if it is under €500.
Withdraw 3 million đồng, about €98, on arrival, in small notes. The 20,000 and 50,000 đồng notes are what street vendors can actually make change for.
Set up your Lumi wallet before departure, so your SEPA transfer has cleared by the time you land.
cardDeclinedVietnam.nextClose: And when a vendor points at that laminated square instead of taking your card, they are not turning you away. They are showing you the system that everyone around you is already using.
