vietnamesePhrases.subtitle: You will not become fluent on an eleven-hour flight. But you can learn the twenty things that decide whether your first week in Vietnam feels like an obstacle course or a holiday.
vietnamesePhrases.author: Tanvi Nag
vietnamesePhrases.imgAlt: A street food cart in Hoi An at dusk, with a Vietnamese chalkboard menu and a VietQR scan-to-pay sign on the counter.
vietnamesePhrases.introP1: The woman at the bánh mì cart on Nguyễn Chí Thanh said a number to me and I heard nothing. Not a word I recognised, not a shape I could guess at. She said it again, slower, kindly. I still had nothing. So I did what everyone does: I held out a handful of notes and let her take what she needed.
vietnamesePhrases.introP2: She took the right amount. Almost everyone will. But I stood there for a second afterwards feeling like a piece of luggage that had wandered into the queue, and that feeling is worth about twenty minutes of preparation to avoid.
vietnamesePhrases.introP3: Here is the honest version of what those twenty minutes should cover. Not "useful travel Vietnamese" in the sense of a phrasebook you will never open. Twenty phrases, in the order you will actually need them, plus the one grammatical fact that matters more than all of them combined.
vietnamesePhrases.pronounH: Start with the word before the words
vietnamesePhrases.pronounP1: Vietnamese has no neutral word for "you." None. You cannot avoid this, because the pronoun sits inside almost every sentence you are about to learn — including "thank you."
vietnamesePhrases.pronounP2: You choose the word based on how old the person looks relative to you. The four that cover nearly everything:

pronouns.gloss: a man around your age or a bit older
a woman around your age or a bit older
a woman / a man of your parents' generation

vietnamesePhrases.pronounP3: You will get this wrong. Everyone gets this wrong, including Vietnamese people meeting someone whose age is hard to read. Nobody minds. What people notice is that you tried, and the difference in how a market vendor responds to "cảm ơn" versus "cảm ơn chị" is not subtle. When you genuinely cannot guess, anh or chị is the safe default — erring slightly older reads as respectful, erring younger does not.
vietnamesePhrases.firstHourH: The six for your first hour

firstHourList.note: Formal, and slightly stiff between friends — but perfect for a stranger, a shop, a hotel desk. Say it on the way in and you have already changed the temperature of the interaction.
The single highest-return phrase in this list. Attach the pronoun.
Barely a word, and you will hear it a hundred times a day. It softens anything it precedes. "Dạ, cảm ơn chị" is warmer than "cảm ơn" alone, and it costs you one syllable.
Also the number zero, and also the word that turns a sentence into a question. It works very hard.
Better than the apologetic smile, because it tells the other person to switch strategies — point, write the number down, show you the screen.
For squeezing past someone, for interrupting, for stepping on a foot on a crowded pavement in the Old Quarter. Which you will.

vietnamesePhrases.moneyP1: This is where a phrasebook usually stops being useful, because the words are only half the problem. The other half is that Vietnamese numbers get abbreviated in speech in a way no textbook mentions.

moneyList.note: Learn this one properly. It opens every transaction that does not have a printed price.
Said with a smile it is an opening move, not an accusation. Said flatly it ends the conversation. Tone of voice does the work here, not vocabulary.

moneyList.gloss: Could you come down a little?
moneyList.note: For markets and souvenir stalls. Not for restaurants, cafés, or anywhere with a menu — haggling over a 50,000₫ bowl of phở (about €1.65) reads as rude, not thrifty.
You will also see people mime a scribble in the air. Both work.

Literally "can I do a bank transfer" — but in practice this is how people ask to pay by QR code, and it is what you say when you spot a laminated QR square taped to the counter. Increasingly the answer is yes even at a pavement noodle stall.
You will mostly hear this said to you, when you hand over a 500,000₫ note for a 25,000₫ coffee. Break large notes at supermarkets and chain cafés, then spend the small ones on the street.

vietnamesePhrases.moneyNote: It is worth knowing why the answer to number eleven is sometimes no. Those squares run on VietQR, Vietnam's national bank transfer network, and the apps that scan them are built around having a Vietnamese bank account. So a visitor can ask the question perfectly and still have no way to follow through. Closing that gap for European travellers is the thing we work on at Lumifin — but the phrase earns its place either way, because the answer also tells you when to reach for cash instead.
vietnamesePhrases.numbersH: Two number habits that will save you real money
vietnamesePhrases.numbersLead1: "k" means thousand, and it is often dropped entirely.
vietnamesePhrases.numbersP1: A price written as 50k is 50,000₫. Spoken, "năm mươi" — fifty — usually means fifty thousand, because nothing costs fifty đồng. Once you accept that everything is in thousands, the numbers get much easier to hold in your head.
vietnamesePhrases.numbersLead2: The 20,000₫ and 500,000₫ notes are both blue.
vietnamesePhrases.numbersP2: This is the most expensive mistake available to a new arrival, and it is a twenty-five-fold one. The 500,000₫ note is slightly larger and a deeper blue-green; the 20,000₫ is paler. Photograph the two side by side on your first day and keep the picture. Vietnamese banknotes are polymer, so they all feel identical in a dark wallet.
vietnamesePhrases.numbersP3: For reference on what things actually cost: bánh mì from a cart runs around 25,000₫ (about €0.85), a bowl of phở 50,000–70,000₫ (€1.65–€2.30), cà phê sữa đá around 25,000₫, and a glass of bia hơi in Hanoi still lands near 10,000₫ (about €0.35). A Grab across Da Nang is usually 40,000–60,000₫.
vietnamesePhrases.foodH: Ordering food without pointing at a stranger's bowl

foodList.note: Pair it with anything: "cho tôi cà phê sữa đá." It is the workhorse construction of eating in Vietnam.
"Cho tôi cái này" plus a finger at the menu will get you fed in any restaurant in the country.
Vietnamese food is generally milder than Thai, but the chilli usually arrives on the side and the bowl of ớt on the table is not a garnish.
Say it to the person who cooked it. Watch what happens.
The most disproportionately valuable sentence in any language.

aroundList.note: For a taxi or a Grab motorbike when the pin has landed somewhere approximate. Point as you say it.
Rarely needed with Grab, occasionally essential with a street taxi in an alley the map does not know about.
Worth asking rather than assuming in either direction. In Da Nang and central Ho Chi Minh City the answer is often yes. In a Hanoi residential ward at 7am, often not.

vietnamesePhrases.tonesH: One thing about tones, and then we'll leave it
vietnamesePhrases.tonesP1: Vietnamese is tonal: six tones in the northern standard, five in most southern speech, where two of them have merged. The same syllable with a different pitch contour is a different word — not a mispronounced version of the same word, a genuinely different one.
vietnamesePhrases.tonesP2: This is why your carefully rehearsed "cảm ơn" occasionally gets a blank look. You did not say it badly. You may have said something else.
vietnamesePhrases.tonesP3: The practical response is not to master the tones before you fly. It is to accept that roughly one attempt in four will not land, and to have a fallback ready: point, show the number on your phone, or hand over the screen. Nobody in Vietnam expects a European visitor to have tones. The attempt is what registers, and the fallback is what gets the transaction done.
vietnamesePhrases.beforeP1: Three things, none of which take longer than a coffee:
beforeList: Screenshot this list and save it to your phone's favourites, so it works with no signal at the airport.
Download the Vietnamese language pack in Google Translate for offline use — the camera mode on a menu is genuinely good.
Learn the pronoun rule on the plane. It is the one item here with compounding returns, and it takes ten minutes.
vietnamesePhrases.beforeClose: Then land, walk up to the first cart you see, and say xin chào. The rest sorts itself out faster than you would think.
vietnamesePhrases.calloutBody: Number eleven is the phrase we think about most. Lumifin lets European travellers pay Vietnam's QR codes from a euro balance — no Vietnamese bank account needed, so "chuyển khoản được không?" can actually end in a payment.

seo.title: What 1,000,000₫ Actually Buys You in Da Nang
seo.description: A full day in Da Nang for 1,000,000₫ (about €33), itemised — room, three meals, scooter, beach and beer, with 2026 prices in đồng and euros.

oneMillionDongDaNang.title: What 1,000,000₫ Actually Buys You in Da Nang
oneMillionDongDaNang.subtitle: About €33. A hotel room, three meals, a scooter, a beach, and a beer — with change. Here is the receipt, and everything that would have blown it.
oneMillionDongDaNang.author: Tanvi Nag
oneMillionDongDaNang.imgAlt: A bowl of mì Quảng noodles with herbs and chilli on a Da Nang table, beside a fan of Vietnamese đồng banknotes.
oneMillionDongDaNang.introP1: A million of anything sounds like a lot until you are holding it. One 500,000₫ note, four 100,000s, a 50 and a couple of 20s, and the stack is thinner than a paperback. That is roughly €33. In Amsterdam it is dinner for one, badly.
oneMillionDongDaNang.introP2: In Da Nang it is a day.
oneMillionDongDaNang.introP3: Not a scraping, hostel-dorm, instant-noodles day either. A good one. I wanted to know exactly where the money went, so I kept every price for twenty-four hours — the way you would if you were arguing with someone about whether Vietnam is really as cheap as people say.
oneMillionDongDaNang.introP4: Here is the whole thing, then the parts worth explaining.

ledgerRows.item: Room, An Thượng, booked three weeks out
The lift, because it was 34 degrees
Bánh tráng cuốn thịt heo, shared

oneMillionDongDaNang.ledgerLeftover: Left over: 25,000₫. Exactly one more iced coffee, which I had.
oneMillionDongDaNang.ledgerRateNote: Rates at roughly 30,200₫ to the euro, which is where things sat as I wrote this. It moves; check it before you rely on it.
oneMillionDongDaNang.roomH: The room is the whole game
oneMillionDongDaNang.roomP1: 380,000₫ for a night is not a mistake and it is not a hostel bunk. It is a small, clean, air-conditioned room in An Thượng, a few streets back from the beach, booked about three weeks ahead. Walk in the same day in December and the same room is 600,000₫ or gone. High season runs December to April and pushes rates up 20–30%.
oneMillionDongDaNang.roomP2: This one line decides everything else. Spend 900,000₫ on a beachfront room and the day is over before breakfast. Spend 380,000₫ and you have 620,000₫ to actually do things with, which in Da Nang is a genuinely large amount of money.
oneMillionDongDaNang.roomP3: Where you put yourself matters almost as much as what you pay. Three areas cover most of it.

areas.name: An Thượng and Mỹ An
areas.body: The foreign long-stay cluster, a few blocks behind Mỹ Khê beach. English everywhere, laundry on every corner, more coffee shops than seems structurally possible. You pay maybe 15% over the city average for the convenience. If it is your first week in Vietnam, this is the sensible landing spot.

areas.name: Hải Châu
areas.body: The actual city centre, west of the river, where the markets and offices are. Cheaper rooms, better and cheaper food, less English, no beach within walking distance. This is where the money goes furthest, and where you will get the most out of the phrases you learned on the plane.

areas.name: The east bank near the Dragon Bridge
areas.body: Splits the difference — walkable to the river, ten minutes from the beach, and priced between the two. Good if you want one evening at the bridge without a taxi.

oneMillionDongDaNang.roomP4: Da Nang is small. The beach strip to the centre is about five kilometres. Almost nothing is more than fifteen minutes from anything else, so the neighbourhood decision is about atmosphere and price, not logistics.
oneMillionDongDaNang.foodH: Food is where Vietnam stops being believable
oneMillionDongDaNang.foodP1: Breakfast was mì Quảng, which is the dish Da Nang argues about most. Turmeric noodles, not quite a soup, a small amount of intensely flavoured broth, pork and shrimp, peanuts, a shard of rice cracker on top. 40,000₫. Street stalls run 30,000₫, a sit-down place with fans and plastic stools runs 40–50,000₫.
oneMillionDongDaNang.foodP2: Lunch was cơm bình dân — the "ordinary rice" places where you point at four or five trays of stuff behind glass and someone builds you a plate. 45,000₫. These are everywhere and they are the single best value in the country. Bánh mì from a cart is 15–25,000₫ if you want to go cheaper still.
oneMillionDongDaNang.foodP3: Dinner was bún chả cá, the fish cake noodle soup that Da Nang does better than anywhere, and then bánh tráng cuốn thịt heo with a group, which is pork belly and herbs you roll yourself in rice paper. That last one was the most expensive food item of the day at 90,000₫ split between people, and it was worth it.
oneMillionDongDaNang.foodP4: Three meals: 130,000₫. Around €4.30. That is not a budget-traveller stunt, that is just what eating locally costs.
oneMillionDongDaNang.foodP5: The number that breaks this is Western food. A brunch in An Thượng — eggs, sourdough, a flat white — lands somewhere between 150,000 and 300,000₫. One of those is two days of local meals. There is nothing wrong with wanting eggs on toast, but it is useful to see what it costs in dishes.
oneMillionDongDaNang.foodP6: If you want to go lower, Chợ Cồn is the answer. It is a covered market, not a tourist one, and the food court at the back does full plates for what a coffee costs in the beach district. Bring small notes; nobody there wants to break a 500,000.
oneMillionDongDaNang.coffeeH: On coffee, which is its own budget line
oneMillionDongDaNang.coffeeP1: Vietnam takes coffee more seriously than most countries take their national sport, and Da Nang has an absurd density of places to drink it. This matters to your budget because the range is enormous.
oneMillionDongDaNang.coffeeP2: A cà phê sữa đá — strong drip coffee over condensed milk and ice — is 20–25,000₫ at a normal Vietnamese café, which is about seventy cents. The same drink in a designer place in An Thượng with air conditioning and a laptop crowd is 55–70,000₫. Both are good. One is three times the other.
oneMillionDongDaNang.coffeeP3: Two worth trying while you are in central Vietnam: cà phê muối, salt coffee, which sounds wrong and is not, and cà phê trứng, egg coffee, which is a whipped yolk custard on top of coffee and is closer to dessert than to a drink. Neither costs more than about 40,000₫ at a local place.
oneMillionDongDaNang.coffeeP4: Three coffees a day at local prices is 60,000₫. Three at expat-café prices is 200,000₫. Over a two-week trip that is the difference of a couple of hundred thousand — not ruinous, but it is a whole extra day.
oneMillionDongDaNang.transportH: Getting around costs almost nothing, and that is the trap
oneMillionDongDaNang.transportP1: 120,000₫ for a scooter for the day, 30,000₫ of petrol, and Da Nang opens up completely: Marble Mountains south, Sơn Trà peninsula north, the Hải Vân Pass if you have the nerve and a full day.
oneMillionDongDaNang.transportP2: The trap is the licence. Renting is trivially easy — a shop will hand you a bike on the strength of a passport photocopy and no questions. Being legal is a different matter, and most travel insurance will not cover a scooter accident if you were riding without the right permit. Vietnam is not a place to find that out experimentally. If you are not certain where you stand, Grab bikes are 25–40,000₫ a hop across town and you will spend maybe 100,000₫ across a whole day.
oneMillionDongDaNang.transportP3: Grab is also worth having simply because it removes the negotiation. The price is on the screen before you get on, which means the airport run — about fifteen minutes to the centre — costs what it costs rather than what someone thinks you will pay.
oneMillionDongDaNang.freeH: The free half of the city
oneMillionDongDaNang.freeP1: A day like this works partly because Da Nang gives a lot away.
oneMillionDongDaNang.freeP2: Mỹ Khê is thirty kilometres of public beach with no entry fee, ever. The 40,000₫ in the ledger is a sunbed, which is optional and which I would skip next time in favour of a towel.
oneMillionDongDaNang.freeP3: The Dragon Bridge breathes fire and sprays water on Friday, Saturday and Sunday nights at 9pm. It is free, there is no ticket, and you should be on the riverside promenade by about half past eight. Monday to Thursday the bridge is just lit up — worth knowing if you are planning which nights to be in town.
oneMillionDongDaNang.freeP4: Sơn Trà peninsula — the forested headland north of the beach — costs nothing but the petrol to ride up it, and the viewpoints looking back over the bay are the best free thing in the city.
oneMillionDongDaNang.freeP5: Marble Mountains is 40,000₫ to enter and another 15,000₫ if you take the lift instead of the steps. In August heat, take the lift.
oneMillionDongDaNang.whenH: When you go changes the number
oneMillionDongDaNang.whenP1: February to May is the sweet spot: dry, clear, warm without being punishing. December through April is also peak season, so the weather you want and the prices you want do not fully overlap — February to April is the compromise most people land on.
oneMillionDongDaNang.whenP2: September to November is the wet end of the year, with typhoons possible in October and November. Rooms get noticeably cheaper. So does everything else. But a washed-out day in Da Nang costs more than a sunny one, not less, because you end up indoors in cafés and restaurants rather than on a free beach. If you go in the rainy months, budget for the weather rather than assuming the low season rate is the whole story.
oneMillionDongDaNang.blowersH: What blows the million in one move
oneMillionDongDaNang.blowersP1: Three things, and they are worth knowing before you plan a week:

blowers.name: Bà Nà Hills — the cable car and the Golden Bridge.
blowers.body: The ticket alone runs 750,000₫ to 1,100,000₫, plus transport. It is a whole day and a whole budget, and it is the single most common way people are surprised by what Da Nang costs.

blowers.name: A proper night out.
blowers.body: Local bia hơi is 10–15,000₫ a glass and keeps everything intact. A rooftop bar is €4–7 a drink and four of them plus a Grab home is your entire day.

blowers.name: Cash withdrawals.
blowers.body: Vietnamese ATMs charge 50–80,000₫ per transaction before your own bank adds anything, and airport exchange counters are worse. Pull out a large amount once rather than a small amount five times, and do not change money at the airport beyond what you need for the taxi.

oneMillionDongDaNang.blowersP2: That last one is quietly the biggest leak in a trip like this. Take out 500,000₫ five times over a week and you have paid roughly a third of a day's budget for the privilege of touching your own money. Most of Da Nang now takes QR payments — the squares taped to every counter, from restaurants to the woman selling mangosteen at Chợ Cồn — but those run on Vietnam's domestic network and generally expect a local bank account, which is the gap we spend our days on at Lumifin. Either way: fewer, larger withdrawals.
oneMillionDongDaNang.blowersP3: One more small thing that costs real money over a week. The 500,000₫ note is what ATMs mostly dispense, and it is close to useless at a market stall or a street kitchen — nobody has change for it. Break the big notes somewhere that can absorb them, like a supermarket or a chain café, and keep a working float of 10s, 20s and 50s. Otherwise you will end up eating somewhere more expensive purely because they could take your money.
oneMillionDongDaNang.levelsP1: The million is one point on a line. Here is roughly where the others sit for one person, one day:

levelsRows.what: Guesthouse or dorm, no scooter, street food only, beach instead of paid sights
Private room, scooter, three sit-down meals, one paid sight
Room with a pool, a Western breakfast, a massage, rooftop drinks
The cable car ticket alone is 750,000–1,100,000₫, before transport or food

oneMillionDongDaNang.levelsP2: Nothing on that list is the right answer. The point is that the gap between the lean day and the comfortable day is about €50, which in most European cities is the gap between two lunches.
oneMillionDongDaNang.verdictH: So is a million a day realistic?
oneMillionDongDaNang.verdictP1: For one person, in shoulder season, eating locally, staying somewhere modest and not doing a big paid attraction — yes, comfortably, and I had change.
oneMillionDongDaNang.verdictP2: For two people it does not double. The room is the same room, the scooter is the same scooter. Two of you land somewhere near 1,400,000₫ for the same day, which is under €25 each.
oneMillionDongDaNang.verdictP3: Over a week it compounds in your favour, because the expensive things are mostly one-offs. Seven days at this level is roughly 6,800,000₫, about €225, and that already includes a paid sight, a scooter every day and three meals out daily. Add one Bà Nà Hills day and one decent night out and you are at €300 for the week, still without cutting anything.
oneMillionDongDaNang.verdictP4: Where it stops working is a high-season room booked late, a week of Western breakfasts, or treating the rooftop bars as normal. None of those are wrong. They are just a different number, and it is better to know that going in than to work it out from your bank app on day four.
oneMillionDongDaNang.verdictP5: If you want the version of this that fits in your head: the room is about 40% of the day, food is about 15%, and everything else is noise. Get the room right and Da Nang is almost hard to overspend in.
oneMillionDongDaNang.calloutBody: A day like this runs on small, frequent payments — and most of them are QR codes now. Lumifin lets European travellers pay Vietnam's VietQR codes from a euro balance, so you are not funding the day through ATM fees.

seo.title: ASEAN QR Cross-Border Payments: What the Linkages Mean for Travellers
seo.description: ASEAN QR cross-border payment links now cover nine countries. What they do, what they don't, and where a European traveller actually stands in 2026.

aseanQrCrossBorder.title: ASEAN QR Cross-Border Payments: What the Linkages Mean for Travellers
aseanQrCrossBorder.subtitle: Nine Southeast Asian countries have started wiring their payment systems together. The volumes are still small, but the direction is clear. Here is what ASEAN QR cross-border payment actually means when you are standing at a food stall.
aseanQrCrossBorder.author: Pierre Lahbabi
aseanQrCrossBorder.imgAlt: A QR payment sticker on a Bangkok night-market food stall, with small payment-system icons along its bottom edge and a phone ready to scan.
aseanQrCrossBorder.ratesNote: Rates in this piece: 1 EUR = 38.5 THB, 30,500 VND and 20,580 IDR, mid-market on 1 September 2026.
aseanQrCrossBorder.stickerP1: At Talad Rot Fai Ratchada in Bangkok, most stalls now have a QR sticker taped somewhere near the till. Look at the bottom edge of one. Under the Thai PromptPay logo there is often a row of smaller marks: DuitNow from Malaysia, PayNow from Singapore, QRIS from Indonesia.
aseanQrCrossBorder.stickerP2: That sticker is not four payment systems. It is one code that four countries have agreed to read.
aseanQrCrossBorder.stickerP3: Watch the queue for a few minutes and you will see it work. A Singaporean couple pays for mango sticky rice, 80 baht or about €2.08, straight from their DBS app. A Jakarta family behind them scans the same square with GoPay and the rupiah leaves their account. Nobody changed money. Nobody touched a card terminal.
aseanQrCrossBorder.stickerP4: Then it is your turn, with a French debit card, and the whole thing stops.
aseanQrCrossBorder.stickerP5: That gap is worth understanding properly, because it is not an accident and it is not going away this year. Here is what has actually been built, and just as importantly, how early it still is.
aseanQrCrossBorder.whatH: What ASEAN QR cross-border payment actually refers to
aseanQrCrossBorder.whatP1: The umbrella name is Regional Payment Connectivity, or RPC. It started as a memorandum signed in November 2022 by the central banks of Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand, and it has grown outward since.
aseanQrCrossBorder.whatP2: The numbers are real, but they are small, and it is worth being honest about that. According to figures cited by the ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office, the region had 29 cross-border payment linkages as of December 2025, carrying 36.2 million transactions worth about US$716.4 million. That works out to roughly US$20 per transaction: a coffee, a plate of noodles, a short taxi ride. Bank Negara Malaysia's governor put ASEAN cross-border QR volume at 12.9 million transactions in the first half of 2025, or around 70,000 a day across the entire region.
aseanQrCrossBorder.whatP3: Set against the domestic QR systems these links connect, which now carry a large share of everyday payments in their home markets, the cross-border layer is a thin bridge. It barely registers next to card spending by tourists.
aseanQrCrossBorder.whatP4: The growth figures need the same caution. The IMF's 2026 analysis of ASEAN digital payments found cross-border QR transactions in Thailand grew more than 300 percent in 2024, and in Malaysia more than 550 percent. Percentages that large usually mean the starting base was tiny. They say less about how big this has become than about how quickly people use it once it exists.
aseanQrCrossBorder.whatP5: That is the signal worth paying attention to. Nobody ran a consumer campaign for these links. Travellers who already paid by QR at home simply kept doing it abroad as soon as they could. Demand for payments that move between local schemes, rather than routing around them through a card network, is plainly there. The infrastructure is what is still catching up.
aseanQrCrossBorder.twoThingsH: Two different things share one name
aseanQrCrossBorder.twoThingsP1: This is where most explanations get muddled, and the distinction matters if you want to read the news accurately.
aseanQrCrossBorder.twoThingsP2: The IMF splits the linkages into two types, and they do different jobs.

linkages.name: QR payment connectivity
linkages.body: Lets you pay a merchant in another country by scanning their code with your home banking app. A Thai visitor in Hanoi scanning a VietQR sheet at a bún chả stall is using this. It is a retail rail, built for tourists and small purchases.

linkages.name: Fund transfer connectivity
linkages.body: Lets you send money to a person in another country using a simple identifier, usually a mobile number or a national ID. PayNow to DuitNow between Singapore and Malaysia is the well-known example. This is a remittance rail, built largely for migrant workers sending wages home.

aseanQrCrossBorder.twoThingsP3: The two often get announced together and reported as one thing. They are not. A country can be linked for merchant payments and not for transfers, or the reverse. When you read that two countries have "linked their payment systems", the useful question is which of the two they linked.
aseanQrCrossBorder.connectedP1: The QR systems already interconnected under RPC include Cambodia's KHQR, Indonesia's QRIS, Lao PDR's Lao QR, Malaysia's DuitNow, the Philippines' QR Ph, Singapore's PayNow, Thailand's PromptPay and Vietnam's VietQR. The network has also reached outside ASEAN: Japan, South Korea and China now sit inside parts of it.
aseanQrCrossBorder.connectedP2: Indonesia is the clearest case to track, because Bank Indonesia publishes its rollout plainly.
aseanQrCrossBorder.connectedP3: The China link shows how quickly usage appears once a corridor opens, even while the totals stay modest. During the sandbox trial with the People's Bank of China that ran from August 2025, Bank Indonesia recorded 1.64 million inbound transactions worth around Rp 556 billion, roughly US$32.1 million, before the service even formally launched.
aseanQrCrossBorder.connectedP4: Bank Indonesia has said it is targeting partnerships with eight countries for cross-border QRIS. India and Saudi Arabia are in discussion. Vietnam, for now, is not a QRIS partner.
aseanQrCrossBorder.whyH: Why central banks built this in the first place
aseanQrCrossBorder.whyP1: The motive matters, because it explains the exclusion better than anything else.
aseanQrCrossBorder.whyP2: Card networks are commercial. Visa and Mastercard want every cardholder in every market, because each one is revenue. These QR rails are the opposite. They are public infrastructure built by central banks, and a central bank's mandate stops at its own residents and its own economy.
aseanQrCrossBorder.whyP3: Two goals drive the work. The first is cost: a domestic instant transfer settles in seconds for a fraction of what a card transaction costs a merchant, and keeping that fee low is a policy choice, not a market outcome. The second is currency. Bank Indonesia places QRIS cross-border explicitly inside its Local Currency Transaction framework, a push to settle regional trade and tourism in rupiah, baht and ringgit instead of routing value through the US dollar. Both Bank Indonesia and the Bank of Thailand have framed this as macroeconomic resilience, not consumer convenience.
aseanQrCrossBorder.whyP4: Thailand moved earliest, with its first cross-border QR link in 2018, four years before the RPC memorandum.
aseanQrCrossBorder.whyP5: Read that way the picture makes more sense. Nobody sat in a meeting and decided to keep Europeans out. These systems were built to serve residents, cut settlement costs and reduce dollar dependency, and a French tourist at a food stall was never the design brief. It also tells you what would have to change: not a tourist policy, but a commercial link between the euro's instant payment system and theirs.
aseanQrCrossBorder.wallH: The wall is your bank account, not your passport
aseanQrCrossBorder.wallP1: Here is the part that trips up almost every traveller who reads about this and expects it to help them.
aseanQrCrossBorder.wallP2: These linkages do not connect countries. They connect domestic instant payment systems. To use one, you need an account inside one of the connected systems, which in practice means a bank account or licensed e-wallet in a participating country, opened with that country's identity documents.
aseanQrCrossBorder.wallP3: The Singaporean at the mango sticky rice stall is not being served because she is Singaporean. She is being served because DBS sits on PayNow, and PayNow has a live link to PromptPay. Her nationality is incidental. Her account is the thing.
aseanQrCrossBorder.wallP4: A European traveller holds a euro account on SEPA, which is a fast and cheap system that happens to be connected to none of this. So the same street code that reads a Malaysian, an Indonesian, a Cambodian and now a Korean app cannot read yours. Not because anyone excluded Europe deliberately, but because nobody has built the link yet.
aseanQrCrossBorder.changesH: What it changes for you even though you cannot use it
aseanQrCrossBorder.changesP1: You are outside the system, but you are not unaffected by it, and this is the practical part.
aseanQrCrossBorder.changesP2: As QR acceptance deepens, cash handling thins out. In Bangkok, Ho Chi Minh City and increasingly Canggu and Seminyak, vendors carry less change than they used to, because most of their customers no longer need any. Handing over a 1,000 baht note (about €26) for a 60 baht purchase is a bigger imposition in 2026 than it was in 2022.
aseanQrCrossBorder.changesP3: Card acceptance is not expanding to fill the gap either. Every year the QR rail gets cheaper and more universal for merchants, the case for renting a card terminal gets weaker. The trend line runs away from your card, not toward it.
aseanQrCrossBorder.changesP4: And the smaller and more local the vendor, the more true all of this becomes. Hotels, airlines and Grab will keep taking your Visa without complaint. A nasi campur warung in Bali charging 45,000 rupiah (about €2.19) almost certainly will not, and has no reason to start.
aseanQrCrossBorder.nexusH: Project Nexus, and the one detail Europeans should watch
aseanQrCrossBorder.nexusP1: The bilateral approach has an obvious ceiling: connecting nine countries pairwise means building a lot of separate links. Project Nexus, run out of the BIS Innovation Hub, is the fix. Each instant payment system connects once to a shared hub and reaches every other participant, instead of negotiating each corridor individually.
aseanQrCrossBorder.nexusP2: Nexus Global Payments was incorporated in Singapore in March 2025 as a not-for-profit to run the scheme. The founding participants are India, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand, with Bank Indonesia as a special observer. Go-live was originally briefed for 2026; current industry reporting points to 2027, which is a normal amount of slippage for infrastructure of this kind.
aseanQrCrossBorder.nexusP3: The detail worth noting: between 2021 and 2024, the BIS ran Nexus proof-of-concept work with the European Central Bank alongside the ASEAN central banks, and an early prototype connected the test systems of the Eurosystem, Malaysia and Singapore. So the technical question of whether euro instant payments could join a network like this has already been answered. It can.
aseanQrCrossBorder.nexusP4: What has not happened is a commercial or political decision to do it, or any published timeline. Treat European access as plausible eventually and absent for your next three trips.
aseanQrCrossBorder.nexusP5: It helps to read all of this as an early chapter rather than a finished system. What exists today is a handful of bilateral bridges carrying small amounts of money. What it proves is more important than what it carries: local payment schemes won at home, travellers want to keep using them abroad, and the missing piece is connectivity between them. Europe's instant payment system is one of those local schemes too.
aseanQrCrossBorder.calloutBody: Lumi is a euro wallet that pays Vietnamese QR codes directly today, with Thailand and Indonesia next, so you can scan the same sticker everyone else in the queue is scanning.
aseanQrCrossBorder.nextP1: If you are travelling in the next 90 days, three things follow from all of the above:

nextItems.name: Stop expecting card acceptance to improve as you go smaller.
nextItems.body: It will not. Plan payment method by vendor size, not by city.

nextItems.name: Carry small notes, not large ones.
nextItems.body: In Thailand break your 1,000 baht notes at a 7-Eleven early. In Vietnam ask for 20,000 and 50,000 dong notes. In Indonesia, 20,000 and 50,000 rupiah.

nextItems.name: Ignore headlines announcing new ASEAN linkages unless a European system is named in them.
nextItems.body: Most of these announcements are genuinely important and have nothing to do with you.

aseanQrCrossBorder.related: We have written separately about how the two systems you will meet most often actually work: <1>VietQR decoded</1> for Vietnam and <2>QRIS decoded</2> for Indonesia.

thailand.problemTitle: The problem with paying in Thailand as a European
thailand.problemP1: Thailand's economy runs on two things: cash and PromptPay. European bank cards are accepted at hotels, malls, and some restaurants — but the vast majority of daily commerce happens outside those places. Street food, tuk-tuks, local markets, temples, laundry services — almost none of these accept foreign cards.
thailand.problemP2: That leaves you with ATMs (220 THB fee per withdrawal, plus your bank's markup) or currency exchange booths (3–8% worse than the real rate). Over a two-week trip, a typical European traveller loses €50–150 just in payment friction.

q1.q: Can I use my European bank card in Thailand?
q1.a: Yes, but expect 1.5–3% foreign transaction fees plus unfavorable exchange rates. Card acceptance is limited outside hotels and tourist areas. Most local vendors, street food stalls, and transport use QR payments or cash.

q2.a: PromptPay is Thailand's national QR payment system, used by over 70 million people. It enables instant transfers between bank accounts and is accepted at millions of merchants — from 7-Eleven to street vendors. Lumi lets European travelers access PromptPay directly.

q3.q: How much do ATM withdrawals cost in Thailand?
q3.a: Thai ATMs charge a flat fee of 220 THB (~€5.50) per withdrawal, plus your European bank typically adds 1.5–3% on top. With withdrawal limits of 20,000–30,000 THB, costs add up quickly over a multi-week trip.

q4.q: Is it better to exchange euros to baht in France or Thailand?
q4.a: Neither is ideal. Airport exchanges in both countries offer poor rates. Bangkok exchanges like SuperRich are better but inconvenient. Lumi gives you near-interbank rates directly through your phone — no physical exchange needed.

q5.a: Download the app, verify your identity, and top up your wallet from your European bank account. Then scan any PromptPay QR code at Thai merchants to pay instantly in baht — at rates significantly better than cards or cash exchanges.

vietnam.subtitle: Navigate the millions of dong, avoid ATM traps, and pay like a local across Vietnam — from Hanoi's Old Quarter to Ho Chi Minh City's street food scene.
vietnam.problemTitle: Why paying in Vietnam is hard for Europeans
vietnam.problemP1: Vietnam is one of the most cash-dependent countries in Southeast Asia for tourists. Card terminals are rare outside international hotels. The currency — Vietnamese dong — comes in denominations that make mental arithmetic a challenge: a 500,000 VND note looks similar to a 20,000 VND note, and the difference is about €18.
vietnam.problemP2: ATMs have low withdrawal limits (often just 2,000,000 VND / ~€74), meaning you'll need multiple transactions per week — each with fees. Meanwhile, the Vietnamese person behind you in line scans a QR code and pays in 2 seconds.

q1.a: Only at upscale hotels, international restaurants, and some shopping centres. The vast majority of Vietnamese commerce — from pho stalls to motorbike taxis — is cash or QR only. Expect 1.5–3% foreign transaction fees where cards are accepted.

q2.a: VietQR is Vietnam's national QR code payment standard, connecting over 40 banks and e-wallets. It enables instant transfers by scanning a single QR code. Adoption has exploded since 2023, with millions of merchants now accepting it — including street vendors and small shops.

indonesia.title: Paying in Indonesia as a European Traveller
indonesia.subtitle: 56 million merchants accept QRIS. Zero of them accept your European bank card. Here's how to bridge the gap — from Bali to Java to Komodo.
indonesia.problemTitle: Why paying in Indonesia is broken for Europeans
indonesia.problemP1: Indonesia has leapfrogged cash with QRIS — a unified QR payment system that works at everything from Jakarta's modern malls to the smallest kaki lima food cart in Yogyakarta. But this system was built for domestic users. To scan a QRIS code, you need either an Indonesian bank account or a local e-wallet like GoPay — both require local ID.
indonesia.problemP2: As a European tourist, you're stuck with ATMs (with withdrawal limits as low as 1,250,000 IDR / ~€70), money changers (where scams are common in tourist areas like Kuta), or your bank card at the handful of places that accept it. Meanwhile, every Indonesian around you is tapping their phone and walking away.

q1.q: Can I use my European bank card in Indonesia?
q1.a: Only at hotels, upscale restaurants, and malls in major cities. The vast majority of Indonesian commerce — warungs, ojeks, local shops, markets — runs on QRIS (QR payments) or cash. Expect 1.5–3% foreign transaction fees where cards are accepted.

q2.a: QRIS (Quick Response Code Indonesian Standard) is Indonesia's national unified QR payment system, launched by Bank Indonesia in 2019. It connects all major e-wallets (GoPay, OVO, Dana, ShopeePay) and banks under one standard. Over 56 million merchants accept it — from Jakarta malls to roadside warungs in Yogyakarta.

q3.q: How much do ATM withdrawals cost in Indonesia?
q3.a: Indonesian ATMs charge 30,000–50,000 IDR (~€1.70–€2.80) per withdrawal. Limits are typically 1,250,000–2,500,000 IDR per transaction (~€70–€140). Your European bank adds 1.5–3% on top. Multiple withdrawals per week add up fast.

q4.q: Why can't Europeans use QRIS directly?
q4.a: QRIS requires either a local Indonesian bank account (needs a KITAS residence permit) or a local e-wallet like GoPay/OVO (needs an Indonesian phone number and ID). European tourists can't access either. Lumi bridges this gap.

q5.a: Download the app, verify your identity, and top up from your European bank. Scan any QRIS code to pay instantly in rupiah — at near-interbank rates. Works at any of the 56+ million QRIS merchants across the archipelago.
